q: Two nurses post identical messages on their personal social-media accounts criticizing the governor's vaccine policy. Rosa works at County General Hospital, which the county owns and operates. Dev works at St. Luke's, a private nonprofit hospital. Each is fired for the post, and each sues under the First Amendment. Both hospitals point out that the Amendment begins “Congress shall make no law.” Which nurse can state a First Amendment claim?
o: Only Rosa: the Fourteenth Amendment applies the First to local governments, but private employers aren't bound.
Neither: by its text, the First Amendment restrains only Congress, so state, local, and private employers fall outside it.
Both: a hospital that serves the public and takes public money is bound by the First Amendment like any government employer.
Only Dev: public employees accept limits on their speech as a condition of government work, so Rosa has waived her claim.
oe: Correct. Incorporation carries the First Amendment to the county (Kennedy cites Cantwell for the Free Exercise Clause), but the Amendment limits only government. Whatever speech policy St. Luke's has adopted is a matter of policy or contract, not the Constitution.
The text says “Congress,” but the Fourteenth Amendment incorporates the First Amendment against state and local governments, including a county hospital.
Serving the public doesn't turn a private employer into the government. The First Amendment binds government, not private actors.
This reverses the rule. Only the public employer is bound by the First Amendment at all, and Kennedy shows a public employee can bring First Amendment claims against the employer.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — State action · incorporation

q: After a resident spreads a false rumor at a public meeting that the city's water is being poisoned, the city council proposes an ordinance making it a misdemeanor to “spread alarming misinformation about public utilities.” One council member opposes it, invoking Justice Brandeis's concurrence in Whitney v. California. Which argument most faithfully reflects that concurrence?
o: The fitting remedy for false and frightening speech is more speech, so the city should answer the rumor with the facts.
Speech may be punished whenever it tends to cause public harm, as long as the legislature has found such a danger.
Free speech is valuable only as a means of finding the truth, so a rumor already shown to be false deserves no protection.
The concurrence carries no weight today, because Brandenburg overruled Whitney and everything said in it.
oe: Correct. Brandeis: the remedy for evil counsels is good ones, not silence coerced by law. He also warned that fear breeds repression and repression breeds hate. The casebook reads the concurrence for these values, not as doctrine.
That describes the Whitney majority's deference to the legislature, which Brandenburg overruled. Brandeis argued the opposite.
Brandeis valued liberty both as an end and as a means. And Alvarez later rejected any general exception for false statements.
Brandenburg overruled the Whitney majority. The Brandeis concurrence survives as a classic statement of First Amendment values, which is how the casebook uses it.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — First Amendment values

q: A state requires public middle-school students to stand each morning and recite a “Civic Creed” that includes the line “I believe that free enterprise is the foundation of liberty.” Maya, a seventh grader, has no religious objection; she refuses because she disagrees with the line politically. The school gives her a one-day detention for each refusal. She sues. What result?
o: Maya wins: the state may not make students declare a belief, and her objection needn't be religious.
The school wins, because Barnette protected only religious objectors like the Jehovah's Witness children who sued there.
The school wins, because a one-day detention is a minor sanction, unlike the expulsions and prosecutions in Barnette.
The school wins if most parents in the district support the creed, because schools may reflect community values.
oe: Correct. Barnette bars any official from prescribing what is orthodox in politics or forcing citizens to confess it by word or act. The holding rests on speech, not religion, so secular objectors are equally protected.
Barnette expressly didn't turn on religious views or their sincerity. A political objection is protected the same way.
The wrong is the compelled declaration of belief, not the size of the penalty. Any sanction for refusing to affirm compels the affirmation.
Fundamental rights “depend on the outcome of no elections,” and majority approval of a message is irrelevant (Barnette; Wooley).
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Compelled affirmation

q: Variation: The school drops the morning recitation. Instead, the civics unit requires students to write a report explaining where the Civic Creed came from and the arguments its supporters make for it. Reports are graded on accuracy, not on whether the student agrees. Maya objects to the assignment. What result?
o: The school wins: it may teach about the creed and its meaning as long as students needn't profess belief in it.
Maya wins, because requiring students to explain an ideology they reject is the same as compelling them to affirm it.
Maya wins, because the creed's political content means the school may not mention it in class at all.
The school wins, because once the recitation ended, students lost any First Amendment protection in the classroom.
oe: Correct. Barnette drew the line between teaching and compelling. The state may teach history and civics, including what a ritual means; it may not compel a declaration of belief.
Explaining arguments isn't adopting them. Barnette expressly allowed the state to acquaint students with the salute and its meaning.
Nothing in Barnette bars teaching about political ideas. The problem was compelled affirmation, which a graded explanation doesn't require.
Students keep their rights in class. The school wins because the assignment teaches rather than compels, not because the right disappears.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Teaching vs. compelling

The school gives her a one-day detention for each refusal. She sues. What result?

q: A state statute requires every public-school student to stand and place a hand over the heart during the national anthem at school assemblies. Students need not sing or say anything. Ben, a high-school junior, stays seated in protest and is suspended. The state argues that the statute regulates only conduct, not speech, so it needs only a rational basis, which the goal of national unity supplies. Should the court accept the state's argument?
o: No. A required gesture of allegiance is a form of utterance, and such a rule can't rest on a rational basis.
Yes. Barnette concerned a spoken pledge, and a silent gesture with no words expresses nothing the Constitution protects.
Yes, because national unity is a compelling interest in wartime and peacetime alike, and this statute is narrowly tailored to it.
No, but only because Ben's protest is political; a student who simply didn't care about the anthem could be compelled.
oe: Correct. Barnette called the salute “a form of utterance” and forbade forcing citizens to confess their faith “by word or act.” Speech may be restricted only to prevent grave and immediate danger. Unity may be pursued by persuasion and example, not compulsion.
Barnette covered the salute as well as the pledge and treated the salute as symbolic speech. A compelled gesture confesses belief “by act.”
Barnette was decided in the middle of World War II and still rejected compelled unity, which “achieves only the unanimity of the graveyard.”
The right not to affirm doesn't depend on the objector's reasons. Barnette protects any objector from a compelled declaration.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Symbolic conduct · level of scrutiny

q: Variation: The hand-over-heart requirement was adopted by statewide referendum with 78 percent of the vote. The state now argues that courts should defer to the people's judgment about how to foster national unity, as the Supreme Court once did in Minersville School District v. Gobitis. How should the court respond?
o: Gobitis was overruled, and fundamental rights depend on the outcome of no elections, so the vote can't save the requirement.
A referendum, unlike an ordinary statute, expresses the direct will of the people and so gets rational-basis review.
The court should defer, because Gobitis remains good law for laws approved directly by the voters rather than by legislatures.
The court should uphold the requirement if the state shows that the referendum was conducted fairly and without fraud.
oe: Correct. Barnette overruled Gobitis's deference to legislatures. The Bill of Rights withdraws certain subjects from political controversy, and that applies equally to a popular vote.
No form of majority approval lowers the scrutiny for compelled affirmation. Barnette rejected that kind of deference.
Barnette overruled Gobitis outright, three years after it was decided.
The fairness of the vote is beside the point. Rights “depend on the outcome of no elections.”
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Counter-majoritarian rights
pre: A state statute requires every public-school student to stand and place a hand over the heart during the national anthem at school assemblies. Students need not sing or say anything. Ben, a high-school junior, stays seated in protest and is suspended. The state argues that the statute regulates only conduct, not speech, so it needs only a rational basis, which the goal of national unity supplies. Should the court accept the state's argument?

q: After each Friday-night football game, a public high school's assistant band director walks to the edge of the field and kneels alone for about thirty seconds of silent prayer while students pack their instruments. No student has joined him, and none has complained. The district orders him to stop, explaining that a reasonable observer would see the prayer as the school's endorsement of religion. He refuses, is suspended, and sues. What is the most likely result?
o: He wins: the district burdened his prayer because it was religious, and quiet private prayer isn't coercion.
The district wins, because a reasonable observer would perceive government endorsement of religion at a school event.
The district wins, because the Establishment Clause takes priority over an employee's free exercise while he is on duty.
The district wins under Smith, because an order to stop praying on the field is neutral and generally applicable.
oe: Correct. Under Kennedy, disciplining an employee's private prayer because it is religious triggers strict scrutiny. The Establishment Clause defense fails: the endorsement test is gone, and brief, quiet prayer that no student joined is not coercion.
Kennedy abandoned Lemon and its endorsement test in favor of history and tradition.
Kennedy held that the clauses are complementary; the Establishment Clause doesn't automatically trump free exercise and speech.
The order targeted the conduct because it was religious, so it isn't neutral. Smith covers only neutral, generally applicable rules.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Private prayer by a school employee

q: Variation: The band director instead gathers the students at midfield after each game, invites them to kneel with him, and leads a spoken prayer. Several students tell the principal they join only because they fear losing their places in the band. The district disciplines him. What is the most likely result?
o: The district wins: leading students in prayer when they feel pressure to join is coercion it may act to avoid.
He wins, because Kennedy treated a coach's prayer at a school athletic event as his private speech, not the school's.
He wins, because the students are high schoolers, whom Kennedy found mature enough to tell permission from endorsement.
He wins, because the history-and-tradition test permits prayer at public events, as it does for legislative prayer.
oe: Correct. Coercion is the core Establishment Clause concern. Kennedy stressed that no students joined and there was no record of pressure; here both facts are reversed, and government may disfavor religion where necessary to avoid an Establishment Clause violation.
Kennedy turned on the quiet, private nature of the prayer and the absence of pressure. It didn't say school employees may lead students in prayer.
Age matters, but Kennedy's point concerned passive observation. Here students are invited, led, and pressured, which is coercion at any age.
Public schools are policed most strictly because they are uniquely coercive. Legislative-prayer traditions don't carry over to leading students in prayer.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Coercion · avoiding a violation

He refuses, is suspended, and sues. What is the most likely result?

q: A school district adds picture books celebrating a range of family structures to its mandatory first-grade reading block. Teachers must use them, and district guidance tells teachers to respond to a student's objection by explaining that the objection is “unkind.” The district allows opt-outs from its health unit and from holiday activities but refuses opt-outs for these books. Parents of several faiths sue for an opt-out. Which analysis is most consistent with current law?
o: Strict scrutiny applies despite the policy's neutrality, and the district's other opt-outs undercut its tailoring.
Smith controls: the policy is neutral and generally applicable, so the parents get no exemption from it.
There is no burden, because mere exposure to ideas doesn't burden religion and Barnette bars only compelled declarations.
There is no burden, because parents who object to the curriculum remain free to choose private school or homeschooling.
oe: Correct. Under Mahmoud, normative instruction of young children by trusted teachers, with correction of dissent, substantially interferes with religious upbringing in the Yoder sense. That triggers strict scrutiny regardless of neutrality, and a robust system of other opt-outs undermines the district's tailoring.
Mahmoud is the Wrinkle 1 exception to Smith. A Yoder-type burden on parents' religious upbringing triggers strict scrutiny even under a neutral, generally applicable policy.
That was the Mahmoud dissent's position. The majority recast Barnette as one egregious example of coercion and held that protection isn't limited to compelled affirmation.
Mahmoud rejected this. Those alternatives are costly, and parents already fund the public schools.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Parental religious upbringing

q: Variation: The same books are assigned in an elective twelfth-grade literature seminar. Teachers present them alongside other novels about family life, ask students to analyze the authors' choices, and give no guidance about correcting students who disagree. Parents of seniors seek an opt-out. How does the analysis change?
o: The parents' claim is much weaker: age, analytical teaching, and no correction point toward mere exposure.
Nothing changes, because Mahmoud requires an opt-out whenever a parent objects to any material on religious grounds.
The parents' claim is stronger, because older students are more likely to adopt the views that the books present.
The claim fails only because the course is an elective; an identical required course for seniors would demand an opt-out.
oe: Correct. Mahmoud called the inquiry fact-intensive: the specific beliefs, the nature of the curriculum, the children's age, and the context. Older students, analytical rather than normative teaching, an elective course, and no correction all cut against a Yoder-type burden.
Mahmoud didn't create an automatic veto. It stressed young children and normative, corrective teaching.
The Court treated youth as heightening the danger, not reducing it. Kennedy likewise trusted high schoolers to tell exposure from endorsement.
Electivity helps, but the other factors (age, descriptive content, no correction) weaken the claim on their own.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Parental religious upbringing · age and context
pre: A school district adds picture books celebrating a range of family structures to its mandatory first-grade reading block. Teachers must use them, and district guidance tells teachers to respond to a student's objection by explaining that the objection is “unkind.” The district allows opt-outs from its health unit and from holiday activities but refuses opt-outs for these books. Parents of several faiths sue for an opt-out. Which analysis is most consistent with current law?

q: A different district adopts a required second-grade unit that presents same-sex families as morally wrong. Parents whose congregation teaches that same-sex marriages are blessed seek an opt-out, citing Mahmoud. The district argues that Mahmoud protects only parents whose faith objects to LGBTQ-inclusive material. Which response best reflects the principle the casebook draws from Mahmoud?
o: The rule must work the same way whichever side objects; if the unit burdens these parents' religious upbringing, strict scrutiny applies.
The district is right, because Mahmoud recognized a burden only for beliefs that the majority described as traditional.
The parents lose, because a curriculum's moral message is the government's own speech, which parents can't challenge.
The parents lose, because parents whose faith supports inclusion aren't burdened by a curriculum that disagrees with them.
oe: Correct. The casebook asks whether you would also grant opt-outs from a curriculum that denigrates LGBTQ people. Doctrine must apply neutrally to similar facts, whichever side wins.
Nothing in Mahmoud's reasoning is limited to one set of religious beliefs, and favoring some beliefs over others would raise its own neutrality problem.
Mahmoud itself let parents challenge a curriculum's normative content. Its rule doesn't depend on which message the school chooses.
A normative curriculum that contradicts a family's faith, taught to young children, is the same kind of burden whichever faith it contradicts.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Applying Mahmoud neutrally

q: Two practices are challenged under the Establishment Clause. (1) Before each lecture, a state-university professor bows her head at her desk for a few seconds of silent prayer, visible to her students. (2) A public kindergarten teacher reads a Bible story to her class every morning and then asks the children what lesson God wants them to learn from it. Which practice most likely violates the Establishment Clause?
o: Only the kindergarten practice: teaching young children religion in class is coercive; quiet private prayer isn't.
Both, because after Kennedy any religious exercise by a government employee in front of students is coercive.
Neither, because Kennedy replaced coercion analysis with a history-and-tradition test that public schools satisfy.
Only the professor's practice, because adult students are more likely to see her prayer as the university's endorsement.
oe: Correct. Public schools are policed most strictly because children are impressionable and schools are uniquely coercive (Engel, Schempp, Edwards). Kennedy holds that an employee's visible, private prayer isn't coercion, and university students are adults.
Kennedy rejected treating visible religious conduct by a teacher as coercive; doing so would be hostility toward religion.
Kennedy read the Establishment Clause through history and tradition but kept coercion as a core prohibition.
This inverts the analysis. Endorsement is no longer the test, and younger students are more vulnerable to coercion, not less.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — The coercion spectrum

q: A state community college requires every new student to attend an orientation session before registering for classes. At the session, students must stand and recite a “Campus Pledge” that ends, “I affirm that diversity is our community's greatest strength.” Leo, age 19, asks to sit silently instead and is told he can't register until he recites it. He sues. What is the strongest response to the college's argument that Barnette protects only schoolchildren?
o: Barnette bars forcing any citizen to confess a belief, and conditioning registration on recitation is that compulsion.
Barnette does protect only schoolchildren, but Leo can win under the Establishment Clause because the pledge is quasi-religious.
Leo wins only if he shows the pledge's message is false, because the state may require affirmation of true statements.
Leo's claim fails if most students agree with the pledge, since reciting it then imposes no real burden on anyone.
oe: Correct. Barnette's rule protects “citizens,” not just children, and Wooley applied the same principle to adults. Tying the pledge to registration leaves no passive option, which makes the compulsion plain.
The pledge is secular. Leo's claim is a compelled-speech claim, which needs no religious hook.
Truth is irrelevant. The state may not prescribe what is orthodox “in politics, nationalism, religion, or other matters of opinion.”
Majority approval is irrelevant (Wooley), and the right not to speak exists precisely for those who disagree.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Compelled affirmation · adults

q: Variation: Orientation is optional, and registration doesn't depend on it. During the session a dean reads the Campus Pledge aloud, and students who wish may join in; others may stay seated and silent. Leo attends, stays seated, and nothing happens to him. He sues anyway. What result?
o: The college wins: no one is forced to profess anything, and the state may voice its own views at an optional event.
Leo wins, because any pledge read by a state official at a public college establishes an unconstitutional orthodoxy.
Leo wins, because Mahmoud rejected the argument that an option to stay out cures a coercive practice.
The college wins, because college students give up the right not to speak when they voluntarily enroll.
oe: Correct. Barnette forbids compelled declaration. With attendance optional and a passive option inside the session, nothing forces a confession by word or act.
Barnette doesn't bar the state from expressing views or holding ceremonies. It bars forcing citizens to affirm them.
Mahmoud rejected telling parents to choose private school. It didn't hold that a truly optional event with a passive option is coercive, and it concerned young children.
Adults keep the right not to speak (Wooley). The college wins because nothing compels Leo, not because he waived anything.
topic: Ch. 1 · Coercion & compelled belief — Compelled affirmation · optional settings
pre: A state community college requires every new student to attend an orientation session before registering for classes. At the session, students must stand and recite a “Campus Pledge” that ends, “I affirm that diversity is our community's greatest strength.” Leo, age 19, asks to sit silently instead and is told he can't register until he recites it. He sues. What is the strongest response to the college's argument that Barnette protects only schoolchildren?

q: A county ordinance requires that all human remains be buried in a licensed cemetery. It applies to everyone, has no exceptions, and was adopted decades ago to protect groundwater. Members of a small faith believe the dead must be buried on family land within a day of death, and they seek an exemption. They bring only a Free Exercise claim. What result?
o: No exemption: a neutral, generally applicable law needn't yield to religious practice it incidentally burdens.
An exemption is required unless the county shows a compelling interest pursued by the least restrictive means.
An exemption is required, because burial practices are religious beliefs, and belief is absolutely protected.
An exemption is required, because a burial practice involves the family, which makes this a hybrid-rights claim.
oe: Correct. Under Smith, the Free Exercise Clause doesn't require exemptions from neutral, generally applicable laws. Belief is absolutely protected; religious conduct is protected only from laws that target it.
That's the pre-Smith approach that RFRA restored by statute. The question limits them to a Free Exercise claim, and Smith rejected strict scrutiny for incidental burdens.
Burial practices are religious conduct. Belief is absolutely protected, but conduct yields to neutral, generally applicable laws.
Smith's hybrid cases paired free exercise with speech, press, or parents' right to direct their children's education. A burial practice doesn't become hybrid just because it involves family.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Neutral, generally applicable laws

q: Variation: The ordinance lets the county health director waive the cemetery requirement “in her sole discretion, for good cause shown.” She has never granted a waiver to anyone. How does that change the analysis?
o: Strict scrutiny now applies, because a discretionary exemption system defeats general applicability even if unused.
Nothing changes, because the director has never granted a waiver, so the law is applied uniformly in practice.
Strict scrutiny applies only if the faith shows the director granted waivers to secular applicants but not religious ones.
Rational basis applies, because a waiver provision makes a law more flexible and so less burdensome to religion.
oe: Correct. Fulton: a mechanism for individualized, discretionary exemptions invites the government to decide which reasons are worthy, so the law isn't generally applicable, whether or not an exemption has ever been granted.
Fulton rejected this argument. The power to grant exemptions is what matters, not its use.
Unequal waivers would be another route (Tandon), but Fulton doesn't require proof that any waiver was granted.
The flexibility is the problem: discretion to excuse some reasons but not others is what defeats general applicability.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — General applicability · discretionary exemptions
pre: A county ordinance requires that all human remains be buried in a licensed cemetery. It applies to everyone, has no exceptions, and was adopted decades ago to protect groundwater. Members of a small faith believe the dead must be buried on family land within a day of death, and they seek an exemption. They bring only a Free Exercise claim. What result?

q: During a future national draft, Owen objects on religious grounds to fighting in one particular war, though not to war in general. The draft law exempts no one on the basis of objections to particular wars, whether secular or religious. Owen claims the Free Exercise Clause entitles him to an exemption. Which authority best supports denying his claim?
o: Smith, which relied on Gillette's refusal to exempt objectors to a particular war from a valid, general draft law.
Lukumi, which held that laws burdening religious conduct are valid whenever they protect public safety.
Fulton, which held that government contracting programs need not make exceptions for religious objectors.
Barnette, which held that the state may require patriotic acts in wartime to preserve national unity.
oe: Correct. Smith grounded its rule in precedents applying valid general laws despite religious motivation: Reynolds (polygamy), Prince (child labor), Braunfeld (Sunday closing), and Gillette (the draft).
Lukumi struck down a law that targeted religious practice. It's the case for laws that aren't neutral, not a basis for upholding one.
Fulton found Philadelphia's policy not generally applicable and ruled for the religious agency.
Barnette held the opposite: even in wartime, the state may not compel affirmation of belief.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Smith's precedents

q: A state statute provides that “no minister, priest, rabbi, imam, or other ordained member of the clergy may serve on the State Utility Commission.” It applies to clergy of every faith equally. Pastor Reyes is nominated to the commission, and the statute blocks her appointment. Which statement best describes her Free Exercise claim?
o: It is strong: the law imposes a special disability because of religious status, which the government may never do.
It fails, because the statute treats all faiths alike and is therefore neutral and generally applicable under Smith.
It fails, because serving on a commission is conduct, and only religious belief is absolutely protected.
It fails, because the state must keep clergy out of government in order to avoid an Establishment Clause violation.
oe: Correct. Smith listed what government may never do: regulate belief as such, compel affirmation, punish doctrines it thinks false, impose special disabilities based on religious status, or take sides in religious disputes.
Neutrality among religions isn't neutrality toward religion. A law that singles out clergy because of their religious status isn't neutral.
The disability is triggered by religious status itself, which Smith placed with belief in the protected core.
Wrinkle 2 lets government disfavor religion only when necessary to avoid an actual Establishment Clause violation. A pastor on a utility commission establishes nothing.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Religious status

q: A city requires anyone going door to door to buy a $50 permit, whether selling products, gathering petition signatures, or proselytizing. Members of a faith that requires them to share their beliefs door to door hand out religious pamphlets without permits and are fined. The city argues that Smith forecloses any Free Exercise claim against a neutral, generally applicable permit rule. What is the members' best response?
o: Their claim pairs free exercise with free speech, the kind of “hybrid” claim Smith distinguished.
Proselytizing is a religious belief, and Smith held that belief is absolutely protected from any regulation.
Smith applies only to criminal prohibitions like Oregon's drug law, not to civil permit requirements.
Every permit requirement for speech is a prior restraint that is invalid without regard to the Religion Clauses.
oe: Correct. Smith explained past exemptions from neutral laws as hybrid cases combining free exercise with another right, such as speech or press, or parents' right to direct their children's education (Yoder). Handing out pamphlets is speech.
Smith listed proselytizing among religious practices, which are protected only against laws that target them. Belief is what's absolutely protected.
Smith's rule isn't limited to criminal statutes. It covers neutral, generally applicable laws of all kinds.
Permit schemes raise speech questions, but content-neutral permit rules aren't automatically invalid. And the city's argument is about Smith, which the hybrid theory answers.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Hybrid rights

q: Soon after a congregation whose worship involves burning herbs indoors opens in town, the council bans “burning any plant material inside a building open to the public,” citing smoke inhalation. The ordinance never mentions religion. It exempts restaurants with wood-fired ovens, cigar bars, hookah lounges, and theatrical smoke effects. The congregation is the only group affected. It sues. What result?
o: The congregation wins: the exemptions spare comparable secular smoke, so strict scrutiny applies, and the law fails it.
The city wins under Smith, because the text doesn't mention religion and applies to everyone who burns plants indoors.
The congregation wins only if it proves that individual council members personally harbored hostility toward its faith.
The city wins, because indoor smoke is a public-health concern and courts defer to a city's health judgments.
oe: Correct. Like Hialeah's ordinances in Lukumi, a facially neutral law gerrymandered by exemptions falls almost entirely on religious practice. Underinclusive for its own stated interest, it fails strict scrutiny.
Facial neutrality isn't enough. Lukumi looks at how the exemptions shape the law's real operation.
Lukumi's gerrymander analysis doesn't require proof of anyone's motive; the pattern of exemptions shows the selective burden.
Under strict scrutiny, health claims get no deference, and leaving restaurants and cigar bars alone shows the law doesn't seriously pursue the interest.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Neutrality · gerrymandered exemptions

q: Variation: At trial, the city argues that there is no religious practice to protect, because the congregation's teachings about the herbs are internally inconsistent and some members also burn the herbs recreationally at home. The members testify, credibly, that indoor burning is central to their worship. How should the court treat the city's argument?
o: Reject it: the test is sincerity, and beliefs needn't be logical or consistent to others.
Accept it, because inconsistent practice proves as a matter of law that the beliefs are not truly religious.
Accept it, because the Free Exercise Clause protects only practices that a faith's official doctrine makes mandatory.
Reject it, but only because the city waived the argument by not raising it before it enacted the ordinance.
oe: Correct. The Free Exercise checklist begins with a sincere religious practice that the government burdens. Lukumi: beliefs need not be “acceptable, logical, consistent, or comprehensible” to others to merit protection.
Courts don't grade the logic or consistency of religious beliefs. Inconsistency might bear on sincerity, but sincerity is established here.
Courts don't decide what a faith requires. The question is whether the practice is sincerely religious.
There is no such waiver rule. The argument fails on the merits.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Sincerity
pre: Soon after a congregation whose worship involves burning herbs indoors opens in town, the council bans “burning any plant material inside a building open to the public,” citing smoke inhalation. The ordinance never mentions religion. It exempts restaurants with wood-fired ovens, cigar bars, hookah lounges, and theatrical smoke effects. The congregation is the only group affected. It sues. What result?

q: A state licensing board revokes the license of a family counselor who, citing her religious beliefs, referred a same-sex couple to a colleague. At the hearing, one board member says that “religion has been the excuse for every act of bigotry in history,” and no one responds. A year earlier, the board took no action against three secular counselors who declined clients on grounds of personal conscience. The counselor sues. Which ruling is most likely?
o: The revocation violates Free Exercise, because the board didn't apply the law with neutrality toward religion.
The revocation stands, because the licensing code is neutral and generally applicable on its face, so Smith controls.
The revocation is void, because the First Amendment exempts religious professionals from antidiscrimination rules.
The revocation stands, because one member's remark can't be attributed to the board as a whole.
oe: Correct. Masterpiece Cakeshop: official hostility (disparaging religion as an excuse for bigotry, unchallenged) and harsher treatment of a religious objection than of comparable secular objections violate the Free Exercise Clause.
Even a neutral law must be applied neutrally. Hostility in its application takes the case outside Smith.
Masterpiece was narrow. It didn't resolve that tension and said states can generally protect gay persons' equal access to goods and services.
In Masterpiece, commissioners' remarks that went unchallenged, together with disparate treatment, showed the body lacked neutrality.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Neutrality in application

q: Variation: No board member says anything about religion, and the board has disciplined every counselor, religious or secular, who declined clients for a reason the code prohibits. What is the most likely result?
o: The revocation likely stands: with no hostility and evenhanded enforcement, Smith governs and no exemption is required.
The revocation is invalid, because Masterpiece holds that religious objectors must be exempted from public-accommodations laws.
The revocation is invalid, because any burden on a counselor's religious practice triggers strict scrutiny.
The revocation stands, but only because counseling is professional speech that gets no First Amendment protection.
oe: Correct. Masterpiece turned on hostility and disparate treatment. Without either, the code is neutral and generally applicable as written and as applied, and the Court said states can generally protect equal access.
Masterpiece expressly declined to decide that broader question.
Under Smith, only burdens imposed by laws that aren't neutral or generally applicable trigger strict scrutiny, absent one of the wrinkles.
That isn't the reason. The Free Exercise claim fails under Smith; any speech claim would need its own analysis.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Neutrality in application
pre: A state licensing board revokes the license of a family counselor who, citing her religious beliefs, referred a same-sex couple to a colleague. At the hearing, one board member says that “religion has been the excuse for every act of bigotry in history,” and no one responds. A year earlier, the board took no action against three secular counselors who declined clients on grounds of personal conscience. The counselor sues. Which ruling is most likely?

q: A state contracts with private agencies to conduct adoption home studies. The contract bars agencies from rejecting prospective parents based on marital status “unless the Secretary, in the Secretary's sole discretion, grants an exception.” No exception has ever been granted. A faith-based agency declines to certify unmarried cohabiting couples, and the state ends its contract. The agency sues. What standard governs?
o: Strict scrutiny, because the Secretary's discretionary exception power makes the policy not generally applicable.
Smith's rule, because no exception has ever been granted and the policy has been applied to every agency alike.
Rational basis, because the state is acting as a contracting party rather than as a regulator of private conduct.
Strict scrutiny, but only if the agency first applies for an exception and is turned down.
oe: Correct. Fulton: a formal mechanism for discretionary, individualized exemptions defeats general applicability even if no exemption has been granted. The government then must satisfy strict scrutiny.
Fulton rejected this. The existence of the exception power, not its use, is what matters.
Fulton applied strict scrutiny to Philadelphia's contract terms; the contracting context didn't lower the standard.
Fulton required no application. The exemption system itself made the policy not generally applicable.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — General applicability · individualized exemptions

q: Variation: Under strict scrutiny, the state argues that it has compelling interests in maximizing the number of adoptive families and in treating all prospective parents equally. How should the court evaluate those interests?
o: By asking whether denying this agency an exception serves a compelling interest; the state's own exceptions undercut that.
By asking whether the interests are compelling in general; if they are, the policy survives as applied to every agency.
By deferring to the state's judgment, because child welfare is an interest of the highest order.
By requiring the agency to prove that an exception would cause no harm to any prospective parent.
oe: Correct. Fulton frames strict scrutiny around the particular claimant. The agency adds families rather than removing them, and an exception system shows the state doesn't treat equal treatment as inviolable.
Strict scrutiny is exemption-specific. Interests stated at a high level of generality don't carry the burden.
Strict scrutiny is not watered down (Tandon). Weighty interests must still justify denying this exemption.
The government bears the burden under strict scrutiny, not the claimant.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Strict scrutiny · this claimant
pre: A state contracts with private agencies to conduct adoption home studies. The contract bars agencies from rejecting prospective parents based on marital status “unless the Secretary, in the Secretary's sole discretion, grants an exception.” No exception has ever been granted. A faith-based agency declines to certify unmarried cohabiting couples, and the state ends its contract. The agency sues. What standard governs?

q: During an outbreak, a state caps indoor worship services at 10 people. Gyms and movie theaters may operate at half capacity, while concerts and sporting events are also capped at 10. The state argues that concerts are the right comparison, since they, like worship, gather large groups for hours, and they are treated the same. It offers no evidence that worship is riskier than a gym session with the same precautions. What standard applies?
o: Strict scrutiny: gyms, a comparable secular activity, are treated better, even though concerts are not.
Smith's rule, because the activities most like worship, concerts and sporting events, face the same cap.
Smith's rule, because the state may reasonably assume that singing and close contact at worship spread disease faster.
Strict scrutiny, but only if the worshippers show that the state was hostile toward religion when it set the caps.
oe: Correct. Tandon: strict scrutiny applies whenever any comparable secular activity is treated more favorably, and it doesn't matter that others are treated as badly. Comparability turns on risk, and the state must show worship is riskier even with the same precautions.
That was the Tandon dissent's “apples and watermelons” argument. The majority rejected it.
The state “cannot assume the worst when people go to worship but assume the best when people go to work.” It must prove the greater risk.
Tandon requires no hostility. Favorable treatment of a comparable secular activity is enough.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Comparable secular activity

q: Variation: The state introduces expert evidence that indoor worship, even with masks and distancing, involves prolonged close contact and group singing that spread the virus far more than gym workouts under the same precautions. How does this evidence matter?
o: It may show gyms aren't comparable, because Tandon measures comparability by risk and lets the state prove a greater one.
It doesn't matter, because any difference in treatment between religious and secular gatherings triggers strict scrutiny.
It doesn't matter, because evidence of risk bears only on whether the state's interest is compelling.
It shows the state may now ban all indoor worship outright, since worship has been proven the riskiest activity.
oe: Correct. Tandon compares activities by the risk they pose to the government's interest. If the state actually shows that worship is riskier even with the same precautions, the gym is no longer a comparable secular activity.
Only comparable secular activities count, and comparability is judged by risk.
Risk evidence bears on comparability, the threshold question, as well as on scrutiny.
A ban singling out worship would target religious exercise and face strict scrutiny on its own terms.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Comparability by risk
pre: During an outbreak, a state caps indoor worship services at 10 people. Gyms and movie theaters may operate at half capacity, while concerts and sporting events are also capped at 10. The state argues that concerts are the right comparison, since they, like worship, gather large groups for hours, and they are treated the same. It offers no evidence that worship is riskier than a gym session with the same precautions. What standard applies?

q: A state requires every driver's-license photo to show the applicant's uncovered head and hairline, citing the accuracy of facial recognition. Applicants who wear head coverings for medical reasons, such as hair loss from chemotherapy, are exempt. Amira wears a headscarf for religious reasons and is refused a license unless she removes it. She brings a Free Exercise claim. What standard applies?
o: Strict scrutiny, because the medical exemption means the rule isn't generally applicable.
Smith's rule, because the photo requirement doesn't mention religion and applies to every applicant.
Strict scrutiny, but only if the legislature exempted medical coverings in order to disadvantage religious applicants.
Rational basis, because driving is a privilege the state may condition on reasonable photo rules.
oe: Correct. A law that exempts comparable secular conduct while refusing religious exemptions isn't generally applicable (Lukumi; Tandon). A medical head covering threatens accurate identification as much as a religious one.
The medical exemption is what matters. Facial neutrality doesn't save a rule that favors comparable secular reasons.
Favoring comparable secular conduct triggers strict scrutiny without proof of a hostile motive.
Calling a license a privilege doesn't lower the standard. The question is whether the rule is neutral and generally applicable.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Secular exemptions

q: Variation: The photo rule has no exceptions at all, and the state enforces it against every applicant who wears any head covering. Amira argues that the federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act requires the state to accommodate her unless it can satisfy strict scrutiny. What result?
o: She loses: the rule is neutral and generally applicable under Smith, and federal RFRA doesn't bind the states.
She wins, because RFRA requires every government in the country to satisfy strict scrutiny before burdening religion.
She wins, because Mahmoud requires strict scrutiny whenever a neutral law substantially burdens religious exercise.
She loses, because Boerne struck down RFRA entirely, so it no longer applies to anyone.
oe: Correct. Without a secular exemption, Smith governs. RFRA requires strict scrutiny of substantial burdens, but City of Boerne v. Flores held it exceeds Congress's power as applied to state and local governments; it binds only the federal government.
Boerne held RFRA unconstitutional as applied to state and local governments.
Mahmoud's exception concerns parents' religious upbringing of their children. It isn't a general return to strict scrutiny.
RFRA still binds the federal government. It just doesn't reach the states.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — No exemptions · RFRA's reach
pre: A state requires every driver's-license photo to show the applicant's uncovered head and hairline, citing the accuracy of facial recognition. Applicants who wear head coverings for medical reasons, such as hair loss from chemotherapy, are exempt. Amira wears a headscarf for religious reasons and is refused a license unless she removes it. She brings a Free Exercise claim. What standard applies?

q: A state's compulsory-attendance law, which has no exemptions, requires every child to attend an accredited school until age 18. Members of a close-knit agrarian faith withdraw their children after eighth grade, believing that high school would pull the children away from the community's way of life. The parents are prosecuted and invoke the Free Exercise Clause. Under the current framework, what standard applies?
o: Strict scrutiny, because the law interferes with the parents' religious upbringing of their children.
Smith's rule, because the law applies to every family and wasn't enacted to target any religion.
Strict scrutiny, but only if the state has granted attendance exemptions to some secular families.
Rational basis, because Dobbs eliminated unenumerated parental rights as a basis for heightened scrutiny.
oe: Correct. This is Wrinkle 1 (Yoder; Mahmoud): strict scrutiny applies to a generally applicable law that interferes with parents' religious education of their children. Smith explained Yoder as resting on parents' right to direct their children's education.
Neutrality isn't enough when the Yoder wrinkle applies. These are essentially Yoder's facts.
Secular exemptions would trigger strict scrutiny by another route, but Wrinkle 1 doesn't depend on them.
The Court is wary of unenumerated rights after Dobbs, so Mahmoud said little about the doctrinal basis, but it still applied strict scrutiny to a Yoder-type burden.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Parental religious education

q: A city policy forbids employees from engaging in “personal activities” in public view while on duty. For years it was never enforced. Then a parks worker is suspended for kneeling briefly to pray during his break, and the supervisor's memo says the suspension was imposed “because the employee's conduct was religious and might offend the public.” The worker sues. What standard most likely applies?
o: Strict scrutiny, because the city admitted acting at least partly because the conduct was religious.
Smith's rule, because on its face the policy bars every kind of personal activity, religious or not.
Rational basis, because avoiding offense to the public is a legitimate goal for any employer.
Strict scrutiny, but only if the worker shows that secular personal activities were tolerated in public view.
oe: Correct. In Kennedy, the district conceded it acted in part because of the religious character of the coach's conduct, so its policy wasn't neutral. A facially neutral rule enforced because conduct is religious isn't neutral in application.
A neutral text doesn't save a policy the government admits it applied because the conduct was religious.
Government may not decide that religious exercise is offensive (Masterpiece, citing Barnette), and the admitted motive triggers strict scrutiny.
Unequal treatment is one route to strict scrutiny, but the city's admission is enough by itself.
topic: Ch. 2 · Free Exercise — Religious motive · facially neutral rule

q: A public high school's student council, elected by the students, chooses a “student chaplain” who delivers a prayer over the stadium's public-address system before every home football game. Attendance at games is voluntary. Separately, after scoring a touchdown, a player kneels briefly in the end zone to pray on his own. A parent challenges both. Which is most likely permissible?
o: Only the player's prayer: the stadium prayer is the school's own religious exercise, while the player's is private.
Both, because the stadium prayer is student-led and nobody is required to attend the games.
Neither, because the Establishment Clause bars all religious expression on public-school property.
Both, because Kennedy replaced the school-prayer precedents with a history-and-tradition test that allows brief prayers.
oe: Correct. Public schools are policed most strictly under the Establishment Clause; Engel struck down even nonmandatory prayer. Individual religious expression at school remains protected (Kennedy).
Engel invalidated school prayer even though participation was voluntary. Running the prayer through the school's system at its own event makes it the school's exercise.
Kennedy rejected that view. Treating private religious expression at school as forbidden would be hostility to religion.
Kennedy didn't overrule the school-prayer cases, and coercion in schools remains a core concern.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Prayer in public schools

q: A county commission opens each meeting with a two-minute prayer by a volunteer member of the local clergy; the volunteers rotate among faiths. On the courthouse lawn stands a 60-year-old granite Ten Commandments monument among other historical markers. A resident sues, arguing that both practices fail the endorsement test, because a reasonable observer would see them as government approval of religion. What is the most likely result?
o: Both are likely permissible, because history and tradition support both practices.
Both are likely invalid, because a reasonable observer would perceive government endorsement of religion.
The monument is permissible, but the prayer is invalid because a prayer is a religious exercise, not a display.
The prayer is permissible, but the monument is invalid because it favors one religious tradition.
oe: Correct. Kennedy abandoned Lemon and the endorsement test. Short legislative prayers and longstanding religious displays are generally allowed on historical grounds, as with the Texas Capitol monument upheld in Van Orden v. Perry.
The endorsement test is no longer the law after Kennedy.
Opening legislative sessions with short prayers is a practice with deep historical roots and is generally allowed.
Longstanding monuments like the one in Van Orden have been upheld on historical grounds.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — History and tradition

q: Variation: By order of the school board, the same monument is installed this year in the main hallway of a public elementary school. What is the most likely result?
o: Likely unconstitutional: schools are policed more strictly, and this display is new.
Valid, because Van Orden upheld the same text, and the history-and-tradition test works the same way everywhere.
Valid, because a passive display asks nothing of students, so it can't coerce them.
Invalid, because Kennedy held that any religious display on government property violates the Establishment Clause.
oe: Correct. The outline notes that public schools are stricter because students are impressionable. A newly installed religious text at the center of an elementary school also lacks the historical pedigree behind the Capitol monument.
Context matters. Schools are treated more strictly than capitol grounds.
Schools are policed strictly precisely because children are impressionable and attendance is mandatory, even when the message is passive.
Kennedy held nothing like that, and longstanding displays are generally allowed.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Displays in public schools
pre: A county commission opens each meeting with a two-minute prayer by a volunteer member of the local clergy; the volunteers rotate among faiths. On the courthouse lawn stands a 60-year-old granite Ten Commandments monument among other historical markers. A resident sues, arguing that both practices fail the endorsement test, because a reasonable observer would see them as government approval of religion. What is the most likely result?

q: A city gives low-income parents tuition vouchers usable at any accredited private school in the city, religious or secular. Because most of the city's private schools are religious, 85 percent of the vouchers are redeemed at religious schools. Taxpayers sue under the Establishment Clause. What result?
o: The program is valid, because the aid reaches religious schools only through parents' genuine and independent choices.
The program is invalid, because most of the money ends up at religious schools.
The program is valid only if the vouchers may not be spent on religious instruction.
The program is required, because the Free Exercise Clause obligates states to fund private education.
oe: Correct. Zelman: aid that reaches religious schools through genuine, independent private choice doesn't violate the Establishment Clause. The government isn't choosing religion; parents are.
Where the choice is genuine and independent, the share that ends up at religious schools doesn't change the analysis.
Zelman imposed no secular-use requirement, and Carson rejected excluding schools because funds would pay for religious instruction.
States needn't subsidize private education at all. They just can't exclude religious schools once they do.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Private-choice aid

q: Variation: The vouchers may be redeemed only at religious schools; secular private schools are excluded. What result?
o: Likely invalid: a religion-only benefit favors religion and isn't neutral private choice.
Valid, because parents still make a genuine choice about which religious school their children attend.
Valid, because after Carson a state may fund religious schools in any way it chooses.
Invalid, but only if a single denomination ends up receiving most of the vouchers that parents redeem.
oe: Correct. Government may not give benefits only to religious entities. Zelman depended on parents choosing among religious and secular options; here the government has made the religious choice for them.
Choice among religious schools doesn't make a religion-only program neutral.
Carson bars excluding religious schools from a general benefit. It doesn't allow benefits reserved for religious schools.
The problem is favoring religion over nonreligion, however the vouchers are spread among faiths.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Benefits only for religion
pre: A city gives low-income parents tuition vouchers usable at any accredited private school in the city, religious or secular. Because most of the city's private schools are religious, 85 percent of the vouchers are redeemed at religious schools. Taxpayers sue under the Establishment Clause. What result?

q: A state offers grants to private nonprofit summer camps for wheelchair ramps and accessible cabins. The program excludes any camp “owned or operated by a church or religious organization.” A Jewish summer camp that otherwise qualifies is denied solely on that ground. Which statement best describes the state's constitutional position?
o: The exclusion likely violates Free Exercise; the state may open the program to all eligible camps or end it.
The exclusion is valid, because “play in the joints” lets states decline to fund religious groups even where funding would be lawful.
The exclusion is valid, because the camp remains free to raise private money for the same improvements.
The exclusion is required, because paying for a religious camp's cabins would establish religion.
oe: Correct. Under Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, and Carson, denying a generally available benefit solely because of religious character triggers the strictest scrutiny. A state needn't fund camps at all, but if it does, it can't exclude religious ones.
That second sense of play in the joints is in retreat; the funding trilogy rejected it.
The ability to raise private funds doesn't cure a penalty imposed because of religious status.
Neutral aid for accessibility isn't an establishment, and the exclusion penalizes free exercise.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Exclusion from public benefits

q: A rural state pays private-school tuition for students whose towns have no public high school, but only at “nonsectarian” schools, defined as schools that don't teach any subject through the lens of a faith. Two families choose an accredited religious school and are denied. The state argues it isn't excluding the school for being religious; it's just declining to pay for religious instruction. What result?
o: The families win: a state that subsidizes private schools can't exclude religious ones, even for religious use.
The state wins, because it may decline to fund religious uses even though it can't exclude schools based on religious status.
The state wins, because its own constitution requires stricter separation than the federal Establishment Clause does.
The families win, but only because the religious school is accredited and teaches the state curriculum.
oe: Correct. Carson rejected the status-versus-use distinction. An interest in separating church and state more strictly than the federal Constitution requires isn't compelling, and Zelman shows that including religious schools wouldn't violate the Establishment Clause.
Carson applied the rule to religious use as well as status.
An interest in stricter separation than the federal Constitution requires isn't compelling (Carson; Wrinkle 2).
Carson didn't depend on the schools following the state curriculum; participating private schools needn't.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Exclusion based on religious use

q: Variation: In response, the legislature ends the tuition program and instead builds regional public high schools with a strictly secular curriculum. Religious families argue that Carson entitles them to keep receiving tuition at religious schools. What result?
o: The state wins: it needn't fund private education at all, and it may keep its public schools strictly secular.
The families win, because ending a program in response to Carson is itself a penalty on religious exercise.
The families win, because Carson requires every state to give religious families a funded alternative to secular public schools.
The state wins, but it must now add religious instruction to the regional schools' curriculum.
oe: Correct. Carson stressed its limits: a state may provide a strictly secular education in its public schools and may end a private-school subsidy altogether. It just can't exclude religious schools from a subsidy it offers.
Carson expressly recognized that the state may end the program.
Carson required nondiscrimination within a program, not the creation of one.
The opposite is true: religious instruction in public schools raises unique Establishment Clause concerns.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Limits of Carson
pre: A rural state pays private-school tuition for students whose towns have no public high school, but only at “nonsectarian” schools, defined as schools that don't teach any subject through the lens of a faith. Two families choose an accredited religious school and are denied. The state argues it isn't excluding the school for being religious; it's just declining to pay for religious instruction. What result?

q: A state defends excluding religious schools from its tuition program by arguing that the program is just a way of providing a free public education, which must be secular. Which additional fact, if true, would most strengthen that argument under Carson?
o: Participating schools must admit all students free of charge, follow the state curriculum, and hire certified teachers.
Most participating schools charge tuition above the state's payment and choose students by entrance exam.
The legislature declared in the statute's preamble that the program provides the equivalent of a public education.
The program has excluded religious schools for over forty years without any legal challenge.
oe: Correct. Carson rejected Maine's “public education” framing because participating schools could be selective, often weren't free, didn't follow the state curriculum, needn't hire certified teachers, and could be single-sex. Erasing those differences makes the benefit look like public education.
These are the very features that made Maine's benefit look like a private-school subsidy rather than public education.
Labels don't control. Carson looked at how the participating schools actually operate.
Maine's exclusion dated to 1981 and still fell. Longevity doesn't change what the benefit is.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Public education vs. private benefit

q: A state's charter schools are created under state law, publicly funded, free, open to all, supervised by a state board, and closable by the state. A Catholic diocese applies to run a religious charter school, and the board denies the application. The diocese sues under the Free Exercise Clause, citing Carson. What is the best assessment?
o: It's unsettled: whether charters are public or private decides it, and the Court split 4–4 in Drummond.
Carson squarely requires the state to approve the application, because charter schools receive public funds.
Drummond held that religious charter schools violate the Establishment Clause, so the denial is required.
The denial is valid, because “play in the joints” still lets states refuse to fund any religious school.
oe: Correct. In Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond (2025), the Court split 4–4, leaving in place a state ruling against a religious charter without setting precedent. Expect the issue to return.
Carson concerned private schools in a tuition program. Whether charters are public or private is the unresolved question.
Drummond was a 4–4 split with no opinion. It affirmed the state ruling without creating precedent.
That sense of play in the joints is in retreat after the funding trilogy; it can't settle the case.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Religious charter schools

q: Two inmates each want to grow a half-inch beard for religious reasons. One is held in a federal prison; the other in a state prison that receives federal funds. Each prison enforces a neutral grooming rule with no exceptions. Where does each inmate have his strongest claim?
o: The federal inmate under RFRA; the state inmate under RLUIPA.
Both inmates under RFRA, which applies to federal, state, and local governments alike.
Both inmates under the Free Exercise Clause, which requires strict scrutiny of grooming rules that burden religion.
Neither, because Smith forbids legislatures to give religious practice more protection than the Constitution does.
oe: Correct. RFRA still binds the federal government after Boerne. RLUIPA, a narrower statute covering land use and institutionalized persons, applies to the states. Both require strict scrutiny even for neutral rules.
City of Boerne v. Flores held that RFRA exceeds Congress's power as applied to state and local governments.
A neutral, generally applicable grooming rule gets no strict scrutiny under Smith. The statutes provide the stronger claims.
Smith left accommodation to the political process. Granting more protection than the Constitution requires is permissible (Cutter).
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — RFRA · RLUIPA

q: Responding to Smith, a state enacts a statute providing that no state law may substantially burden a person's religious exercise unless the state shows a compelling interest pursued by the least restrictive means. A taxpayer sues, arguing that the statute violates the Establishment Clause by giving religious believers a benefit that others don't get. What result?
o: The statute is likely valid: government may accommodate religion beyond what the Free Exercise Clause requires.
The statute is invalid, because it gives religious believers a benefit that nonbelievers can't get.
The statute is invalid, because Boerne held that RFRA-type statutes violate the Establishment Clause.
The statute is valid only if it gives secular conscientious objectors the same exemptions.
oe: Correct. This is the first, still-living sense of “play in the joints.” Cutter unanimously upheld RLUIPA on this basis: accommodations needn't come packaged with secular benefits, though courts must weigh the burdens on nonbeneficiaries.
Lifting a government-imposed burden on religious exercise is accommodation, which Cutter allows. The bar on religion-only benefits concerns subsidies, not accommodations.
Boerne held that Congress lacked power to impose RFRA on the states. A state may adopt the same standard for itself.
Cutter held that accommodations needn't come packaged with benefits for secular beliefs.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Accommodation · play in the joints

q: Variation: The state instead passes a narrower law giving every employee an absolute right to refuse work on his or her chosen Sabbath, with no exception for hardship to the employer or the burden on coworkers who must cover the shifts. What is the strongest Establishment Clause objection?
o: An accommodation that ignores its costs to others can become unlawful fostering of religion.
Any accommodation of religion in private employment violates the Establishment Clause.
The law is invalid because Smith forbids states to protect religious conduct by statute.
The law is invalid because it regulates private employers, who aren't bound by the First Amendment.
oe: Correct. Cutter upheld accommodation but warned that it can become unlawful “fostering” of religion, so courts must account for burdens on nonbeneficiaries. Hobby Lobby showed how real those third-party costs can be.
Accommodation beyond what the Free Exercise Clause requires is generally permissible (Cutter; RFRA).
Smith left room for legislative accommodation.
The law is state action. The question is whether the state's accommodation goes too far, not whether employers are bound.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Burdens on nonbeneficiaries
pre: Responding to Smith, a state enacts a statute providing that no state law may substantially burden a person's religious exercise unless the state shows a compelling interest pursued by the least restrictive means. A taxpayer sues, arguing that the statute violates the Establishment Clause by giving religious believers a benefit that others don't get. What result?

q: A family-owned, closely held manufacturing company objects on religious grounds to a new federal regulation requiring employers to cover a particular medical procedure in their employee health plans. The government argues that a for-profit corporation can't exercise religion and that, in any event, its employees' interests should control. Under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, what is the best assessment?
o: The company may invoke RFRA, as closely held corporations did in Hobby Lobby, though costs to employees matter.
The company can't invoke RFRA, because only individuals and nonprofit religious groups can exercise religion.
The company's only claim is under the Free Exercise Clause, and Smith dooms it if the regulation is neutral.
The company wins outright, because RFRA exempts religious objectors from federal laws that burden them.
oe: Correct. Hobby Lobby (5–4) held that RFRA covers closely held for-profit corporations with religious owners and exempted them from the contraceptive mandate. The case illustrates accommodation's costs to third parties.
Hobby Lobby rejected that limit for closely held corporations.
RFRA supplies strict scrutiny against the federal government even for neutral rules.
RFRA requires strict scrutiny of substantial burdens; the government can still prevail if it satisfies that test.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — RFRA and for-profit corporations

q: A ninth-grade world-history unit on religion has two parts. In the first, students read short descriptive excerpts from several traditions and write a summary of each. In the second, the class must take part in a guided meditation led by a visiting monk and recite a short Buddhist chant together. Parents object to the unit. Which part is most vulnerable to challenge?
o: The chant and meditation, which make students perform a religious exercise rather than study one.
The readings, because exposing students to religious texts in a public school violates the Establishment Clause.
Neither part, because ninth graders can tell teaching about religion from endorsing it, as Kennedy held.
Both parts equally, because Mahmoud requires an opt-out from any unit that mentions religion.
oe: Correct. Teaching about religion descriptively is permissible; the outline's world-religions problem favors districts on that kind of content. Requiring students to perform a religious exercise is the coercion and indoctrination that public schools may not impose.
Descriptive study of religious texts isn't indoctrination. The world-religions problem treats it as the district's strongest ground.
Kennedy concerned students passively observing a coach's private prayer, not students being made to perform a religious exercise.
Mahmoud turned on normative content, young children, and correction of dissent, not on any mention of religion.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Religion in the curriculum

q: A state exempts from its sales tax “Bibles, Qurans, Torahs, and other sacred scriptures,” but not other books. A secular publisher sues. The state defends the exemption as a neutral accommodation, since it covers the scriptures of every faith. What is the most likely result?
o: The exemption is likely invalid, because government may not give benefits like tax exemptions only to religious materials.
The exemption is valid, because it favors no particular sect and treats every religion's scripture alike.
The exemption is valid as an accommodation, which Cutter says needn't come packaged with secular benefits.
The exemption is valid, because the history-and-tradition test lets government acknowledge religion's role in society.
oe: Correct. One broadly agreed Establishment Clause rule is that government can't give benefits, such as tax exemptions, only to religious entities. Covering every faith doesn't cure favoring religion over nonreligion.
Evenhandedness among religions doesn't answer favoritism of religion over nonreligion.
Accommodation lifts a government-imposed burden on religious exercise. Paying an ordinary sales tax on a book isn't that kind of burden; this is a subsidy.
Ceremonial acknowledgment and old monuments are one thing; a tax subsidy limited to religious texts is a benefit only for religion.
topic: Ch. 2 · Establishment, funding & RFRA — Establishment Clause core

q: A state requires every home on a state-maintained rural mail route to display on its mailbox a state-issued sticker reading “Proud of Our Heritage.” The state says the sticker promotes state pride and helps carriers spot route mailboxes. Hal, who thinks the slogan glorifies a painful history, covers it with tape and is fined. He sues. What result?
o: Hal wins: the state can't make him display its ideological slogan, and numbers would mark mailboxes.
The state wins, because displaying a sticker is passive and so isn't compelled speech the way a salute is.
The state wins, because most residents approve of the slogan, and it expresses no religious view.
The state wins, because helping mail carriers identify route mailboxes is a compelling interest.
oe: Correct. Wooley: the state may not make a person the courier of its ideological message on private property for the public to see. State pride is an ideological interest, and identification doesn't require a slogan, so the rule isn't narrowly tailored.
Wooley held that passive display differs from a salute only “in degree.”
Majority approval is irrelevant, and Wooley protects any objector, religious or not.
The interest may be legitimate, but it doesn't require an ideological slogan; numbers would do.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Compelled speech · passive display

q: Variation: The sticker shows only the route number and box number in plain type. Hal covers it because he dislikes government markings on his property. What result?
o: The state likely wins: a plain identifying number carries no ideological message, so Hal isn't the state's courier.
Hal wins, because any display the government requires on private property is compelled speech.
Hal wins, because a homeowner's objection needn't be ideological to trigger strict scrutiny.
The state wins, because property owners have no right to refuse any message the state chooses.
oe: Correct. Wooley objected to forcing a person to carry the state's ideological message. In Wooley itself, plate numbers were the narrowly tailored way to identify vehicles.
Wooley distinguished the ideological motto from identifying numbers, which serve identification without ideology.
The objector's reasons don't matter, but the display must convey a message. A route number doesn't.
Wooley gives property owners exactly that right against the state's ideological messages.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Compelled speech · identification
pre: A state requires every home on a state-maintained rural mail route to display on its mailbox a state-issued sticker reading “Proud of Our Heritage.” The state says the sticker promotes state pride and helps carriers spot route mailboxes. Hal, who thinks the slogan glorifies a painful history, covers it with tape and is fined. He sues. What result?

q: Relying on Wooley v. Maynard, an atheist sues to remove “In God We Trust” from U.S. currency, arguing that carrying money forces her to display a religious message, just as driving forced the Maynards to display New Hampshire's motto. What is the strongest response?
o: Wooley distinguished currency: it passes hand to hand and isn't tied to its bearer.
Wooley squarely held that “In God We Trust” on currency is constitutional.
Wooley protects only religious objectors, so an atheist's objection to a religious motto isn't covered.
The compelled-speech rule binds the states but not Congress's choice of national symbols.
oe: Correct. Wooley's footnote 15 distinguished currency, which isn't readily associated with its bearer the way a car is with its driver. The Supreme Court hasn't decided the question, but circuits uphold the motto (Newdow v. Peterson).
Footnote 15 distinguished currency without deciding the question.
Wooley's speech rationale protects any objector, religious or not.
The First Amendment applies directly to Congress; there's no such limit.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Wooley's footnote 15

q: A city adopts two rules for gas stations. Rule 1 requires each pump to show the fuel's octane rating. Rule 2 requires each station to display a poster reading, “This business supports the Mayor's Clean City Pledge.” A station owner challenges both as compelled speech. Which rule is most vulnerable?
o: Rule 2: it compels an ideological message, while factual commercial disclosures are generally allowed.
Rule 1, because any compelled statement, even a factual one, gets the same strict scrutiny as an ideological motto.
Neither, because a business operating under a government license has no right not to speak.
Both equally, because each requires the owner to display government-written words on private property.
oe: Correct. Compelled speech is almost never permitted, but compelled commercial disclosures, like nutrition labels and drug side effects, are the main exception (Ch. 8). An endorsement of the mayor's program is an ideological message under Wooley.
Factual commercial disclosures are the main exception to the rule against compelled speech.
A license doesn't let the government force a business to carry its ideological message.
What the words say matters more than who wrote them: factual disclosure versus ideological endorsement.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Compelled speech · commercial disclosures

q: A town where many survivors of a recent genocide have resettled bans demonstrations “displaying the symbols of any regime that committed genocide” within 1,000 feet of the community center. A fringe group plans a peaceful 20-minute march with those symbols on the public sidewalk past the center on a Saturday afternoon. The town calls the ordinance a reasonable time, place, and manner rule that protects survivors from severe psychological trauma. What result?
o: The ordinance is invalid: it turns on the march's message, and listeners' trauma doesn't justify that.
The ordinance is valid, because it is limited to a 1,000-foot zone and so is a time, place, and manner rule.
The ordinance is valid, because carrying symbols and flags is conduct, not speech.
The ordinance is valid, because speech that traumatizes survivors is a recognized unprotected category.
oe: Correct. Collin v. Smith: a rule triggered by who is marching and what their symbols say is content-based, not a TPM rule. Psychic trauma can't be separated from the anger speech provokes, and residents aren't a captive audience; they can avoid the area for 20 minutes.
