A geographic limit doesn't make a rule content-neutral. This one applies only to certain symbols.
Uniforms, flags, placards, and marching are symbolic speech and assembly.
There's no such category. Collin rejected a trauma exception, and Stevens bars creating new ones.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Content-based restrictions · offense

q: Variation: Instead of a daytime march, the group announces that it will stand outside particular survivors' homes at 2 a.m. with bullhorns, night after night. May the town now act?
o: Yes, through content-neutral rules that protect people in their homes.
No, because Collin held that any restriction on the group's demonstrations would be ideological tyranny.
Yes, and the town may now ban the group's symbols everywhere in town, since the group has shown an intent to harass.
No, because the homeowners can simply go to another room, so they aren't a captive audience.
oe: Correct. Collin recognized that government may protect listeners from intrusions into the home or on a truly captive audience. A content-neutral limit on amplified sound at night (Ch. 9) gets more lenient review.
Collin condemned content-based suppression, not neutral rules protecting the home.
Targeting homes permits neutral rules about homes, not a townwide ban on a message.
The home is the classic place where unwilling listeners can't escape. That's why it gets protection.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Captive audiences and the home
pre: A town where many survivors of a recent genocide have resettled bans demonstrations “displaying the symbols of any regime that committed genocide” within 1,000 feet of the community center. A fringe group plans a peaceful 20-minute march with those symbols on the public sidewalk past the center on a Saturday afternoon. The town calls the ordinance a reasonable time, place, and manner rule that protects survivors from severe psychological trauma. What result?

q: Citing studies showing that young people who play such games grow more hostile to police, a state bans the sale of “video games that portray law-enforcement officers as villains.” Games portraying officers as heroes remain legal. The state's evidence of harm is strong and unrebutted. A game publisher sues. What is the most likely result?
o: The ban is invalid: it favors one viewpoint about police and silences the other, even if the harm is real.
The ban is valid, because the state has proved real harm, which satisfies strict scrutiny.
The ban is valid, because video games are entertainment rather than political speech.
The ban is valid, because it applies to every game publisher alike and so is content-neutral.
oe: Correct. Hudnut: government may not declare one perspective right and silence its opponents, even accepting that the disfavored speech causes real social harm. The harm only shows the power of speech.
Hudnut accepted the city's harm premise and still struck the ordinance as viewpoint discrimination.
Brown held that video games are speech; it is “difficult to distinguish politics from entertainment, and dangerous to try.”
Applying to every speaker doesn't make a law neutral. This one turns on the game's viewpoint.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Viewpoint discrimination

q: After lengthy hearings, a state legislature finds that speech demeaning a person's race has negligible value compared with the harm it causes. It declares such speech a new unprotected category, punishable whenever a jury finds the speech demeaning. A defendant is convicted for a racist speech at a rally in a park. What is the strongest argument for reversal?
o: Legislatures may not create unprotected categories by weighing a kind of speech's value against its costs.
The legislature's findings weren't detailed enough to show that the speech's harms outweigh its value.
The law covers only race, when it should also have covered religion, sex, and other traits.
The speech occurred in a public park, where time, place, and manner rules don't apply.
oe: Correct. Stevens rejected this “startling and dangerous” categorical balancing. Content-based restrictions are allowed only in historically recognized categories, and hate speech is generally protected (Collin; R.A.V.).
Better findings wouldn't help. The balancing method itself is forbidden.
Broadening the list wouldn't cure a category created by balancing.
Parks are subject to neutral TPM rules (Ch. 9). The problem is the content-based ban.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — No new unprotected categories

q: A state makes it a crime to knowingly make a false statement about one's military service “at any public meeting.” At a city council meeting, Grant falsely claims to have served as a Navy SEAL. He seeks no money or other benefit. The state argues that, unlike the Stolen Valor Act in Alvarez, its law is limited to public meetings. Under the Alvarez plurality, what result?
o: Unconstitutional: the law still targets falsity and nothing more, and counterspeech can expose the lie.
Constitutional, because limiting the law to public meetings cures the breadth that doomed the Stolen Valor Act.
Constitutional, because knowingly false statements of fact have no value and are unprotected.
Unconstitutional, but only because the statute doesn't require that the speaker knew the statement was false.
oe: Correct. Alvarez rejected any general exception for false statements; lies are punishable when tied to legally cognizable harm such as fraud or defamation. A content-based ban on lies must be “actually necessary,” and truth is the ordinary remedy.
Breadth was one problem in Alvarez, but the core defect is punishing falsity with no cognizable harm.
Falsehood loses protection when it is tied to cognizable harm, such as defamation or fraud, not merely because it is false.
The statute does require knowledge. The problem is what it punishes.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — False statements

q: Variation: Grant makes the same claim to a retiree while asking her to donate $5,000 to his “veterans' relief fund,” which he keeps for himself. He is prosecuted under a general fraud statute. What result?
o: He may be convicted: fraud is an unprotected category, because the lie is used to take money.
He can't be convicted, because Alvarez held that lies about military service are protected.
He can't be convicted unless the government shows that counterspeech couldn't have prevented the harm.
He may be convicted only under a statute that specifically targets lies about military service.
oe: Correct. Alvarez distinguished false statements tied to legally cognizable harm, like fraud, which is one of the historically unprotected categories. “Make no law” isn't absolute.
Alvarez protected lies that sought no material gain. Lies used to take money are fraud.
Fraud is unprotected, so strict scrutiny's “actually necessary” requirement doesn't apply.
A general fraud statute suffices. The category is fraud, not military lies.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Fraud · cognizable harm
pre: A state makes it a crime to knowingly make a false statement about one's military service “at any public meeting.” At a city council meeting, Grant falsely claims to have served as a Navy SEAL. He seeks no money or other benefit. The state argues that, unlike the Stolen Valor Act in Alvarez, its law is limited to public meetings. Under the Alvarez plurality, what result?

q: In a Supreme Court case, four Justices join an opinion holding a statute unconstitutional under strict scrutiny. Two Justices “concur in the judgment,” finding the statute unconstitutional under intermediate scrutiny. Three dissent. A lower court later faces a similar statute. What did the case establish?
o: That the statute was invalid; but the four-Justice reasoning is a plurality, which usually isn't binding as such.
A binding rule that strict scrutiny applies, because the plurality opinion drew the most votes.
A binding rule that intermediate scrutiny applies, because six Justices agreed the statute was invalid.
Nothing at all, because a decision without a majority opinion has no effect, even on the parties.
oe: Correct. A majority opinion needs five Justices joining the reasoning, and concurring in the judgment means agreeing only with the result. Alvarez had this structure: Kennedy's plurality applied strict scrutiny; Breyer and Kagan concurred in the judgment under intermediate scrutiny.
Four votes are fewer than the five needed for a majority on the reasoning.
Six Justices agreed on the result, but only two applied intermediate scrutiny; that isn't a majority for the reasoning.
The judgment, supported by six Justices, decides the case. Only the reasoning lacks majority support.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Reading split decisions

q: City A bans all picketing within 150 feet of a school during school hours. City B bans picketing within 150 feet of a school during school hours “except peaceful picketing about a labor dispute involving the school.” A group picketing about school-board policy is cited in each city. Which statement is correct?
o: City B's rule is content-based because it turns on the picket's subject; City A's is content-neutral.
Both rules are content-neutral, because neither singles out a particular viewpoint on school-board policy.
City B's rule is easier to defend, because it allows more speech than City A's total ban.
Both rules are content-based, because any restriction on picketing affects what picketers can say.
oe: Correct. Mosley: government has no power to restrict expression because of its subject matter. An exemption that requires reading the sign's topic makes a rule content-based. A rule about time, place, and manner alone is content-neutral and gets more lenient review (Ch. 9).
A rule can be content-based without being viewpoint-based. Favoring labor picketing discriminates by subject matter.
Allowing more speech doesn't help if the line is drawn by content. The exemption is what makes B suspect.
Rules about when and where, applied to all messages alike, are content-neutral.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — Content-based vs. content-neutral

q: After Stevens struck down 18 U.S.C. § 48, Congress considers four replacement bills aimed at crush videos. Which is most likely to survive a First Amendment challenge?
o: A ban limited to obscene crush videos, tying it to an existing category.
A ban on all depictions of animal cruelty, with a broader exception for works of “serious value.”
The original statute, paired with a Justice Department promise to charge only extreme cruelty.
A statute declaring depictions of animal cruelty low-value speech, subject only to rational-basis review.
oe: Correct. Stevens left open a statute limited to crush videos or extreme cruelty. Tying the ban to obscenity, an existing category, avoids creating a new one. Congress's 2010 crush-video law took this approach (beyond the casebook).
A broader exception still leaves a content-based ban on protected depictions, and there's no historical tradition of banning depictions of animal cruelty.
The First Amendment doesn't leave us “at the mercy of noblesse oblige.” Courts construe the text, not enforcement promises.
Calling speech low-value is a description, not a test. Stevens rejects categorical balancing.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech framework — After Stevens

q: Kane sells stolen credit-card numbers on a dark-web forum and is charged under a statute that makes it a crime to “publish any financial account information belonging to another person.” He concedes his own speech is unprotected, but argues that the statute also covers journalists who publish leaked bank records of public officials and consumer advocates who post examples of exposed data. Which statement is most accurate?
o: He may raise overbreadth but must show substantial, realistic protected applications.
He can't raise other people's rights, because litigants may challenge a law only as applied to their own conduct.
He wins if he can identify a single protected application of the statute, however unlikely.
He must show that the statute has no valid application at all, as in any facial challenge.
oe: Correct. Overbreadth lets a litigant whose own speech is unprotected assert others' rights. Because it is “strong medicine,” Hansen requires realistic unconstitutional applications and a lopsided ratio to the statute's plainly legitimate sweep.
Overbreadth is the exception to that rule; it exists because overbroad laws chill speakers who never come to court.
Fanciful hypotheticals don't count, and a single application isn't substantial.
That's the ordinary facial-challenge standard (Salerno). Overbreadth is a separate, more forgiving First Amendment doctrine.
topic: Chs. 3, 5 · Overbreadth & vagueness — Overbreadth

q: A federal statute makes it a crime to “encourage, counsel, or induce” any person to evade federal income taxes. At a rally, Dana tells the crowd, “The income tax is illegitimate. Nobody should pay it.” She is charged and moves to dismiss, arguing that the statute is overbroad because “encourage” reaches pure advocacy. Applying Hansen, how should the court proceed?
o: Read the verbs as terms of art for soliciting or aiding specific crimes, which excludes Dana's advocacy.
Give “encourage” its ordinary meaning, which reaches Dana's speech, and strike the statute down as overbroad.
Uphold the charge, because urging people to break the law is unprotected speech.
Rewrite the statute to cover only tax schemes involving fraud, since courts may narrow any statute to save it.
oe: Correct. Hansen read “encourage or induce” as terms of art covering intentional solicitation and facilitation of specific unlawful acts. A fairly possible constitutional reading must be adopted, and general advocacy falls outside it (compare Williams; Brandenburg).
Hansen chose the specialized criminal-law meaning, partly through constitutional avoidance, rather than everyday usage.
Abstract advocacy of lawbreaking is protected unless it meets Brandenburg; soliciting a specific crime is different.
Avoidance chooses between fair readings; it doesn't let courts rewrite the text.
topic: Chs. 3, 5 · Overbreadth & vagueness — Construction · terms of art

q: A city ordinance provides: “Whoever displays any image depicting nudity in a place visible from a public street shall be fined.” Charged for displaying a classical nude painting in a gallery window, the gallery owner challenges the ordinance as overbroad. The city asks the court to read “any image depicting nudity” to mean only obscene images, and it promises to prosecute only obscene displays. What should the court do?
o: Judge the ordinance as written: avoidance can't override clear text, and a promise of restraint doesn't save an overbroad law.
Adopt the city's narrow reading, because a court must choose whatever interpretation saves a statute.
Accept the city's promise, because prosecutors' charging policies define a statute's reach for overbreadth purposes.
Dismiss the challenge until the city actually prosecutes someone for a non-obscene display.
oe: Correct. The avoidance canon picks the constitutional reading only when a statute can fairly be read two ways; it doesn't override unambiguous text (Hansen). And under Stevens, the First Amendment doesn't leave speakers “at the mercy of noblesse oblige.”
Only a fairly possible reading may be adopted, and “any image depicting nudity” can't fairly mean “obscene images.”
Stevens rejected exactly this argument: courts construe the text, not the government's enforcement policy.
The owner has already been charged for a non-obscene painting, and overbreadth exists to prevent chilling before it happens.
topic: Chs. 3, 5 · Overbreadth & vagueness — Avoidance · enforcement promises

q: A statute bans selling “any depiction of an animal being shot” if the shooting was illegal where the depiction is sold, with an exception for works of serious educational value. A defendant convicted for selling videos of illegal dogfights that end in shootings challenges the statute as overbroad. Which fact most strongly supports the challenge?
o: The plain terms reach a large market in hunting videos sold where such hunting is restricted.
A law professor can imagine a documentary about poaching that a prosecutor might theoretically charge.
The defendant's own videos showed real animal cruelty that was illegal everywhere.
The government has promised to prosecute only videos depicting cruelty, never hunting.
oe: Correct. In Stevens, realistic and numerous protected applications, like hunting videos sold where hunting is restricted, dwarfed the legitimate sweep. That lopsided ratio made the law substantially overbroad.
Overbreadth requires realistic applications, not fanciful ones (Hansen).
That puts his conduct within the legitimate sweep; it doesn't support the challenge.
Enforcement promises are irrelevant to overbreadth (Stevens).
topic: Chs. 3, 5 · Overbreadth & vagueness — Overbreadth · the ratio

q: Two laws are challenged as void for vagueness. Law 1 makes it a crime to “loiter on a public sidewalk in a manner offensive to passersby.” Law 2 makes it a crime to offer material “in a manner that reflects the belief” that it depicts real minors engaged in sexual conduct. Which law is more likely void for vagueness?
o: Law 1, because “offensive to passersby” is a subjective standard that gives no fair notice and invites arbitrary enforcement.
Law 2, because a person's belief can't be observed, so no one can know in advance what is prohibited.
Both, because any law reaching speech must define each of its terms with mathematical precision.
Neither, because vagueness is a First Amendment doctrine that applies only to laws that are also overbroad.
oe: Correct. Vagueness concerns uncertainty about what fact must be proved, as with standards like “annoying” or “indecent.” Williams held that belief is a true-or-false fact; that it may be hard to prove is a job for the reasonable-doubt standard.
Difficulty of proof isn't vagueness. Whether someone held a belief is a clear question of fact (Williams).
Perfect clarity isn't required. The test is fair notice and standards that prevent seriously discriminatory enforcement.
Vagueness comes from the Due Process Clause and is a separate doctrine from overbreadth.
topic: Chs. 3, 5 · Overbreadth & vagueness — Vagueness

q: Variation: The city amends Law 1 to bar “standing on a public sidewalk so as to block pedestrians and force them into the street.” Is the amended law vague?
o: No: it describes objective conduct that an ordinary person can recognize and an officer can verify.
Yes, because close cases, such as partly blocking a sidewalk, will still arise.
Yes, because any law regulating how people use a sidewalk is inherently standardless.
No, but only because the amendment also makes the law content-neutral.
oe: Correct. The amendment replaces a subjective reaction (“offensive”) with an observable fact (blocking passage), which gives fair notice and limits enforcement discretion.
Close cases don't make a law vague; the reasonable-doubt standard handles them (Williams).
Clear, objective standards for sidewalk use are not vague.
Content neutrality is a different question. The law is no longer vague because its terms are objective.
topic: Chs. 3, 5 · Overbreadth & vagueness — Curing vagueness
pre: Two laws are challenged as void for vagueness. Law 1 makes it a crime to “loiter on a public sidewalk in a manner offensive to passersby.” Law 2 makes it a crime to offer material “in a manner that reflects the belief” that it depicts real minors engaged in sexual conduct. Which law is more likely void for vagueness?

q: Ruiz is charged under a statute barring “training” for designated terrorist organizations after he teaches a designated group's members to assemble rifles. He concedes his conduct is clearly covered, but argues that the statute is unconstitutionally vague because it's unclear whether it would reach a professor who teaches the same group about international law. How should the court treat his vagueness argument?
o: Reject it: his own conduct is clearly covered, and concern for others belongs to overbreadth.
Accept it, because in First Amendment cases vagueness lets litigants assert third parties' rights.
Accept it, because any uncertainty in a statute's application makes it void for every defendant.
Reject it, because laws involving national security are immune from vagueness challenges.
oe: Correct. Vagueness focuses on fair notice as to the litigant's own conduct (Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project). Concern for others' protected speech is the business of overbreadth, a First Amendment doctrine.
Vagueness comes from the Due Process Clause, and even in speech cases it looks to the litigant's own conduct. Asserting third parties' rights is a feature of overbreadth.
Uncertainty at the margins doesn't invalidate a law as applied to clearly covered conduct.
There is no such immunity. The argument fails because his own conduct is clearly covered.
topic: Chs. 3, 5 · Overbreadth & vagueness — Vagueness · whose conduct

q: On a political forum, an anonymous user posts: “Someday soon, the people will rise up and burn down that corrupt state legislature.” Thousands of people read the post; nothing happens. The poster is identified and prosecuted under a statute punishing incitement to violence. What is the strongest defense?
o: It urged violence at an indefinite future time, so it wasn't incitement to imminent lawless action.
The post is political speech criticizing the legislature, which gets the First Amendment's highest protection.
The post was anonymous, and anonymous speakers can't be prosecuted for incitement.
The state must show a clear and present danger, and a single online post can't create one.
oe: Correct. Brandenburg requires speech directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it. “Someday soon,” posted to a scattered online audience, satisfies neither. Advocacy of future violence is protected (compare Hess v. Indiana, beyond the casebook).
Political speech is strongly protected, but it can still be punished if it meets the Brandenburg test. The better defense is that this post doesn't.
Anonymity doesn't immunize incitement. The defect is the lack of imminence and likelihood.
Clear and present danger is the older test, replaced in practice by Brandenburg, and the defense doesn't depend on the medium.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Incitement · imminence

q: Variation: At a protest outside a construction site, an organizer with a megaphone tells about 200 people standing at the locked gate, many carrying bolt cutters: “The guards just left. Cut the locks now and wreck the equipment!” Several protesters do so. The organizer is prosecuted. What result?
o: Conviction is proper: the speech was aimed at producing immediate lawless action and was likely to produce it.
Conviction is improper, because the organizer didn't personally cut any locks or damage anything.
Conviction is improper, because protest against a construction project is core political speech.
Conviction is proper, but only because the crowd actually damaged the equipment.
oe: Correct. Every Brandenburg element is met: intent (a direct command), imminence (“now”), lawless action (destroying property), and likelihood (an equipped crowd at the gate).
Incitement punishes the speech itself when Brandenburg is satisfied; the speaker needn't act.
Political context doesn't protect speech that meets the incitement test.
Likelihood is required, but actual violence isn't an element. The speech was punishable when spoken.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Incitement · all four elements
pre: On a political forum, an anonymous user posts: “Someday soon, the people will rise up and burn down that corrupt state legislature.” Thousands of people read the post; nothing happens. The poster is identified and prosecuted under a statute punishing incitement to violence. What is the strongest defense?

q: Cole gives an inflammatory speech denouncing a religious minority to a packed hall while an angry crowd gathers outside, and scuffles break out. He is convicted of disorderly conduct after the judge instructs the jury that it may convict if his speech “stirred the public to anger, invited dispute, or caused unrest.” Cole's lawyer didn't object to the instruction. On appeal, what is the most likely result?
o: Reversal, because the instruction let the jury convict for protected speech.
Affirmance, because the scuffles outside show that the speech actually produced violence.
Affirmance, because speech attacking a religious minority falls outside First Amendment protection.
Affirmance, because the lawyer's failure to object means the instruction can't be challenged on appeal.
oe: Correct. Terminiello reversed on similar facts: speech may not be punished for stirring anger, inviting dispute, or creating unrest. The reading tip is to start with the law as construed; this instruction swept in protected speech.
Because the instruction allowed conviction on protected grounds, the verdict can't stand even if a properly instructed jury might have convicted.
Hate speech is generally protected. It may be punished only if it fits a narrow category like incitement.
That was the Terminiello dissent's point; the majority reversed anyway.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Breach of the peace · start with the law

q: A state statute makes it a felony “to advocate the duty, necessity, or propriety of violence as a means of political reform.” Under it, Dale is convicted for shouting “Storm the doors right now!” to an armed mob outside a courthouse as the mob surged forward. On appeal, Dale argues that the statute is unconstitutional on its face. What result?
o: Dale likely wins, because the statute punishes mere advocacy and he may raise its overbreadth.
Dale loses, because his own speech was incitement, so he can't complain about the statute's reach to others.
Dale loses, because the statute is valid as long as it is applied only to speech that meets the Brandenburg test.
Dale wins, because no statute may ever punish speech that advocates violence.
oe: Correct. Brandenburg struck down Ohio's statute because it punished mere advocacy, with no requirement of intent, imminence, or likelihood. Overbreadth lets a defendant whose own speech could be punished under a narrower law challenge a statute that sweeps in protected speech.
Overbreadth is the exception that lets him do so (Stevens; Hansen).
The statute's text reaches abstract advocacy, so it is invalid on its face. Courts don't rewrite it to save it.
A statute properly limited to Brandenburg incitement would be valid.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Incitement statutes · facial challenges

q: A prosecutor defending a conviction for distributing leaflets that urge resistance to a military draft relies on Abrams, Schaefer, Pierce, and Whitney v. California. She argues that leaflets with a tendency to obstruct recruitment may be punished. How should the court respond?
o: Those cases used clear-and-present-danger and bad-tendency tests that Brandenburg replaced, and Whitney was overruled.
Those cases still control whenever the nation is at war, because Brandenburg applies only in peacetime.
Whitney remains good law, because Justice Brandeis's famous concurrence agreed with the result.
Those cases are still binding, because the Court has never formally repudiated the clear-and-present-danger test.
oe: Correct. The World War I–era cases used clear and present danger to affirm dissidents' convictions, and Whitney upheld punishing mere advocacy. Brandenburg overruled Whitney and requires intent, imminence, and likelihood; Black and Douglas would have rejected clear and present danger expressly.
Brandenburg has no wartime exception, and Douglas stressed how easily the old test crushed dissent even in war.
The concurrence is read for its values, not its doctrine, and Brandenburg overruled the Whitney majority.
Brandenburg replaced it in practice, and Whitney was expressly overruled.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — From clear and present danger to Brandenburg

q: A city charges four people under an ordinance punishing “fighting words.” Which charge is the city's strongest?
o: A man jabs a stranger at a bus stop and spits personal slurs in his face, daring him to swing.
A student wears a backpack patch reading “[Expletive] the Administration” around campus.
A street preacher tells passersby that they are all sinners headed for eternal punishment.
A blogger posts a stream of crude, personal insults about a state senator on a widely read political site.
oe: Correct. Fighting words are personally abusive epithets aimed face to face at a particular person and inherently likely to provoke an immediate violent response (Chaplinsky; Cohen). Even so, the Court hasn't upheld a restriction on this theory since 1942.
Like Cohen's jacket, this is not a direct personal insult to anyone present.
General condemnation of a crowd isn't a personally abusive epithet aimed at a particular listener.
Online insults about someone who isn't present can't provoke an immediate face-to-face fight.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Fighting words

q: A small group marches peacefully down a city street in support of a controversial cause. A larger counter-crowd gathers, shouts threats, and throws a few bottles. Forty officers are on the scene, enough to keep the two groups apart, but the police chief orders the marchers to disperse instead. They refuse and are convicted of failing to obey a dispersal order. What result on appeal?
o: Reversal, because police could control the crowd, and hecklers don't get a veto.
Affirmance, because the march produced imminent violence and so falls within Brandenburg.
Affirmance, because police may always order a dispersal when public safety is at risk.
Affirmance, because the marchers' message was provocative enough to make the crowd's reaction foreseeable.
oe: Correct. There is no heckler's veto. In Cox v. Louisiana and Edwards v. South Carolina, convictions of peaceful protesters were reversed where police could control the hostile crowd.
The violence came from the audience, not from anything the marchers urged. Brandenburg concerns speakers who incite.
Not when the risk comes from hecklers whom police can control; that lets the crowd veto the speech.
A foreseeable hostile reaction is the heckler's veto itself; it doesn't justify silencing the speakers.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Hostile audiences

q: Variation: Only four officers are on the scene. The city manager later admits that he had time to send more officers before the march but chose not to. Does that change the result?
o: No: when the government could have provided protection, its own shortfall can't justify silencing the speakers.
Yes, because with only four officers on hand the police genuinely couldn't control the crowd.
Yes, because speakers are responsible for arranging enough security for controversial events.
No, because the heckler's-veto rule applies however many officers are, or could be, available.
oe: Correct. In Edwards, the city manager admitted he had time to get more police; any shortfall was the department's fault. The heckler's-veto rule still protects the marchers.
The shortfall was self-created. The government can't rely on a shortage it chose.
The cases put the duty to protect speakers on the government, not on speakers to buy protection.
The cases turned on whether police could control the crowd. The point here is that the city could have.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Hostile audiences · police shortfalls
pre: A small group marches peacefully down a city street in support of a controversial cause. A larger counter-crowd gathers, shouts threats, and throws a few bottles. Forty officers are on the scene, enough to keep the two groups apart, but the police chief orders the marchers to disperse instead. They refuse and are convicted of failing to obey a dispersal order. What result on appeal?

q: A county ordinance punishes “fighting words that insult or provoke violence on the basis of a person's disability or age.” It is construed to reach only fighting words. Ezra is charged after shouting a disability slur, face to face, at a man in a wheelchair while daring him to fight. Ezra challenges the ordinance. What result?
o: The ordinance is invalid on its face: the county may ban fighting words but may not single out a subset by topic.
The ordinance is valid, because fighting words are unprotected, so any regulation of them gets only rational-basis review.
The ordinance is valid as applied to Ezra, because his own words were genuine fighting words.
The ordinance would be valid if it also covered race, religion, and gender, as St. Paul's did.
oe: Correct. R.A.V.: unprotected categories aren't “invisible to the Constitution.” Government may regulate them because of what makes them proscribable, but may not pick out a topic-based subset. This ordinance leaves equally provocative fighting words on other topics untouched.
R.A.V. rejected this view of unprotected categories.
R.A.V. struck St. Paul's ordinance on its face, even though the cross burning could be punished under other laws.
St. Paul's ordinance listed those topics and still fell. Adding topics doesn't cure topic-based selection.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Subsets of unprotected categories

q: At a rally outside a factory, a union leader says: “If management doesn't settle by Friday, we'll shut this place down, and anyone who crosses our line will regret it.” Two days later, some workers slash the tires on replacement workers' cars. The leader is prosecuted for incitement. What is the most likely result?
o: Acquittal, because a conditional statement about a future deadline isn't incitement to imminent action.
Conviction, because violence actually followed, which proves the speech was likely to produce lawless action.
Conviction, because “shut this place down” is a call for lawless action.
Acquittal, because speech in a labor dispute is exempt from incitement law.
oe: Correct. Brandenburg requires imminence. A statement tied to a future deadline, followed by violence days later, isn't incitement to imminent lawless action. Emotionally charged rhetoric stays protected even when violence follows (NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware, beyond the casebook).
Likelihood alone isn't enough; Brandenburg also requires intent and imminence.
Shutting a plant down by striking isn't necessarily lawless, and the statement was conditional and about the future.
No kind of speech is exempt from Brandenburg; this speech simply doesn't satisfy it.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Conditional, future statements

q: An activist livestreams outside a courthouse: “We need to shut this courthouse down today.” As people in the crowd begin pushing the barricades, she adds, “I'm not telling anyone to hurt anybody, but history remembers people who act.” Ten minutes later, a group breaks through and damages the entrance. She is charged with incitement. Which additional fact would most strengthen the prosecution's case?
o: That morning she texted a co-organizer, “Once they're at the barricades, I'll push them to break through.”
Her livestream reached 80,000 viewers, most of them watching from home in other states.
She had harshly criticized the presiding judge on social media for months.
She later told reporters that she “didn't mean for anyone to break anything.”
oe: Correct. The courthouse problem is close and turns on intent. Evidence that her words were planned to produce the breach shows they were “directed to” inciting it.
A scattered online audience cuts against imminence and likelihood; it doesn't help the prosecution.
Criticism of a judge is core protected speech and doesn't show an intent to produce imminent lawless action.
A disclaimer helps the defense, not the prosecution.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Incitement · proving intent

q: A state supreme court is asked to abolish the fighting-words doctrine under the state constitution. Which argument tracks the 1993 Harvard Law Review note discussed in the casebook?
o: It rewards fighting back and lets police target minorities and police critics.
The doctrine should be expanded to speech that frightens listeners into fleeing, not just speech that provokes fights.
The doctrine should be replaced with case-by-case balancing of an insult's value against its harm.
The doctrine should be limited to racial slurs, which are the insults most likely to provoke violence.
oe: Correct. The note argues that Chaplinsky should be overruled rather than expanded: punching back isn't something the law should condone (unlike fleeing a false cry of “Fire!”), and the doctrine invites arrests of minorities and critics of the police.
The note rejects expansion, including proposals to add a “fright or flight” response, and argues for eliminating the doctrine.
Stevens forbids that kind of balancing, and the note seeks abolition, not a new test.
A topic-based subset would raise the R.A.V. problem, and the note argues for abolition.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement & fighting words — Critiques of fighting words

q: A state public-nuisance law lets a court permanently enjoin any periodical found to have regularly published “malicious, scandalous, and defamatory” material. The publisher may resume only by persuading the judge that future issues will be proper. A court enjoins a weekly paper that accused the county sheriff of protecting gambling rings. What result on appeal?
o: The injunction is an invalid prior restraint: it stops publication in advance, which the Framers especially opposed.
The injunction is valid, because defamation is unprotected, so a court may stop it before it is published.
The injunction is valid, because the paper can resume publishing once it satisfies the judge.
The injunction is valid unless the paper proves that its accusations were true.
oe: Correct. Near v. Minnesota reversed an injunction on nearly these facts. A prior restraint carries a heavy presumption of invalidity, and the remedy for defamation is an after-the-fact libel suit.
Even unprotected speech is generally dealt with after publication, not by enjoining future issues.
Requiring a judge's approval before publishing is the essence of censorship.
Prior-restraint doctrine puts the heavy burden on the government, not on the publisher.
topic: Ch. 4 · Prior restraints — Prior restraint

q: Variation: Instead of seeking an injunction, the sheriff sues the paper for libel after the articles run, seeking damages for specific false statements. Is that a prior restraint?
o: No: a libel suit punishes speech after publication rather than stopping it in advance.
Yes, because the threat of damages deters the paper from publishing future articles.
Yes, because any judicial action against a newspaper is treated as a prior restraint.
No, and the paper has no First Amendment defense at all, because defamation is wholly unprotected.
oe: Correct. A prior restraint stops speech before it occurs; a damages suit punishes it afterward. Defamation is unprotected only in certain circumstances (the NYT v. Sullivan line, Ch. 7), so the suit has its own First Amendment limits.
Chilling is a real concern, but a damages suit is a later punishment, not a prior restraint.
Courts may decide libel claims after publication; only orders that block speech in advance are prior restraints.
Defamation is unprotected only in certain circumstances (Ch. 7).
topic: Ch. 4 · Prior restraints — Prior restraint vs. later punishment
pre: A state public-nuisance law lets a court permanently enjoin any periodical found to have regularly published “malicious, scandalous, and defamatory” material. The publisher may resume only by persuading the judge that future issues will be proper. A court enjoins a weekly paper that accused the county sheriff of protecting gambling rings. What result on appeal?

q: A newspaper obtains a leaked classified report on a covert program that ended a decade ago. The report shows that officials misled Congress about the program's cost and failure. The government seeks an injunction, offering an affidavit that publication “could damage diplomatic relations and national security” and arguing that the executive branch is best placed to judge that risk. What result?
o: Injunction denied: a general claim of harm to national security doesn't carry the government's heavy burden.
Injunction granted, because the government need show only a real likelihood of grave harm, and the executive's judgment deserves deference.
Injunction granted, because the report was classified and was leaked in violation of law.
Injunction granted, because only a prior restraint can prevent the harm, while later punishment comes too late.
oe: Correct. In the Pentagon Papers case, the heavy presumption against prior restraints wasn't overcome by generalized national-security claims. Black and Douglas called “security” a vague generality.
That was the government's argument in its Pentagon Papers brief, and it lost.
The Pentagon Papers were classified and leaked too.
The government made this argument as well. It doesn't overcome the presumption.
topic: Ch. 4 · Prior restraints — National security

q: Variation: The newspaper instead plans to publish the encryption keys currently used for battlefield communications and the locations of special-forces units now operating abroad. What is the best assessment?
o: It's the strongest case for restraint, within Near's wartime dictum, though none has been upheld.
The injunction must be denied, because the Pentagon Papers case held that no prior restraint is ever permissible.
The injunction must be granted, because any classified information about the military falls within the Near exception.
The injunction must be denied, because the information bears on public debate about the war.
oe: Correct. Near suggested that publishing troop locations might be restrained, and the ACLU's Pentagon Papers brief would allow restraint only for tactical operations, weapons designs, and codes. Still, the Court has never actually upheld such a restraint.
The per curiam applied a heavy presumption, not an absolute bar. Only Black and Douglas took the absolutist view.
Near's dictum is narrow, covering things like troop locations and sailing dates, not anything classified.
Encryption keys and current unit locations are tactical details, not information that bears on policy debates.
topic: Ch. 4 · Prior restraints — The Near exception
pre: A newspaper obtains a leaked classified report on a covert program that ended a decade ago. The report shows that officials misled Congress about the program's cost and failure. The government seeks an injunction, offering an affidavit that publication “could damage diplomatic relations and national security” and arguing that the executive branch is best placed to judge that risk. What result?

q: A former intelligence analyst signed an employment agreement promising to submit anything she writes about her work for prepublication review. She writes a memoir about her agency without submitting it. The government sues to enforce the agreement. What is the best assessment?
o: The government likely prevails, because courts have enforced such secrecy agreements.
The government loses, because the Pentagon Papers case bars every prior restraint involving national security.
The government loses, because agreements to give up First Amendment rights are void.
The government prevails only if the memoir reveals troop movements in wartime.
oe: Correct. Marchetti upheld a restraint based on a signed secrecy agreement, and in Snepp the proceeds of a book published in breach went to the government. Both rest on the agreement.
The Pentagon Papers case involved newspapers that had signed no secrecy agreement.
Courts have enforced these agreements (Marchetti; Snepp).
The agreement, not Near's wartime dictum, is the basis for relief.
topic: Ch. 4 · Prior restraints — Secrecy agreements

q: Variation: The analyst gives her manuscript to a national newspaper, which never signed any agreement and plans to publish excerpts. The government seeks to enjoin the newspaper. What is the best assessment?
o: The paper isn't bound by her contract, so the usual heavy presumption applies.
The newspaper may be enjoined, because it knowingly received material obtained in breach of a contract.
The newspaper prevails because the Press Clause gives institutional media greater rights than the analyst has.
The newspaper may be enjoined, because the government's interest in enforcing secrecy agreements is compelling.
oe: Correct. Marchetti and Snepp rested on the employees' own agreements. A restraint against a newspaper that never signed one is an ordinary prior restraint, governed by Near and the Pentagon Papers case.
The Pentagon Papers were also leaked in breach of obligations, and the injunctions were denied.
The Court treats the press as having the same rights as everyone else. The paper prevails because it isn't a party to the agreement.
An interest in enforcing the analyst's contract doesn't bind a stranger to it, and generalized security claims don't meet the heavy burden.
topic: Ch. 4 · Prior restraints — Secrecy agreements · the press
pre: A former intelligence analyst signed an employment agreement promising to submit anything she writes about her work for prepublication review. She writes a memoir about her agency without submitting it. The government sues to enforce the agreement. What is the best assessment?

q: A state legislature considers two responses to the publication of leaked police misconduct files: (1) a procedure for courts to enjoin publication of such files at the state's request; or (2) a criminal penalty for publishing them, imposed after a jury trial. Which explanation best states why option (1) faces greater constitutional hostility?
o: It stops speech before the public hears it, by a stroke of a pen, without a trial's safeguards and with little public scrutiny.
Injunctions are content-based, while criminal penalties for publication are content-neutral.
Criminal penalties after publication raise no First Amendment concern, so option (2) needs no justification.
Injunctions bind only the press, which gets special protection under the Press Clause.
oe: Correct. Emerson's reasons: prior restraints sweep more broadly, stop speech before it occurs, can be imposed by a stroke of a pen, lack criminal-process safeguards, operate with little public scrutiny, and drive toward excess.
Both options target the files' content; the difference is timing and process.
Penalties after publication are also suspect; they're just less dangerous than prior restraints.
The press has the same rights as everyone; the hostility to prior restraints protects all speakers.
topic: Ch. 4 · Prior restraints — Why prior restraints are worse

q: Over several weeks, Ivan posts repeatedly on a city council member's public page: “I know where your kids go to school. Tick tock.” He testifies that he meant it as a dark joke about her slow response to school-safety complaints. Friends had warned him that people would read the posts as threats, and he kept posting. He is prosecuted for making threats. Under Counterman, what must the state prove?
o: That the posts were objectively threatening and that Ivan was at least reckless about how they'd be read.
That Ivan acted with the purpose of making the council member fear that he would commit violence.
Only that a reasonable person would understand the posts as threatening, whatever Ivan himself was actually thinking.
That Ivan knew to a practical certainty that the council member would take the posts as threats.
oe: Correct. Counterman keeps the objective definition of a true threat and adds a subjective floor of recklessness. His friends' warnings are strong evidence that he knew of the risk and disregarded it.
Purpose was the standard favored by Justice Sotomayor's concurrence. The majority required only recklessness.
That purely objective test was the dissent's view (Barrett, Thomas). The majority rejected it.
Knowledge is more than the First Amendment requires. Recklessness suffices.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — True threats · mental state

q: Variation: Ivan was convicted under a statute requiring only that “a reasonable person would feel threatened” by the communication. The jury was never asked about Ivan's state of mind. What result on appeal?
o: The conviction can't stand, because the First Amendment requires proof that he was at least reckless.
The conviction stands, because the evidence would have supported a finding of recklessness anyway.
The conviction stands, because true threats, like other unprotected categories, are judged by an objective test.
The conviction can't stand, because the state must prove that Ivan intended to carry out the threatened violence.
oe: Correct. That is what happened in Counterman: a conviction under a purely objective stalking standard was vacated and remanded.
The jury never made that finding. The instructions let it convict on a constitutionally insufficient basis.
That was the dissent's argument in Counterman.
A true threat doesn't require intent to carry it out; the required mental state is recklessness about how the words would be understood.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — True threats · objective statutes
pre: Over several weeks, Ivan posts repeatedly on a city council member's public page: “I know where your kids go to school. Tick tock.” He testifies that he meant it as a dark joke about her slow response to school-safety complaints. Friends had warned him that people would read the posts as threats, and he kept posting. He is prosecuted for making threats. Under Counterman, what must the state prove?

q: In a group chat for their fantasy-football league, Pete writes to his longtime friend Sam: “If you trade away my quarterback, I'll strangle you with my bare hands lol.” Sam, irritated, forwards the message to police, and Pete is charged with making a threat. What is the strongest defense?
o: In context, no reasonable recipient would take it as a serious threat of violence.
Online messages can't be true threats, because they lack the immediacy of face-to-face speech.
Pete can't be convicted unless he actually planned to harm Sam.
Messages about sports fall outside the true-threats category because of their subject.
oe: Correct. “True” threats exclude jests and hyperbole, like “I'll kill you if you leave dirty dishes in the sink.” A joking exchange between friends over a game, flagged “lol,” isn't a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence.
Counterman itself involved online messages.
A true threat doesn't require intent to carry it out; the defense is that this wasn't a serious threat at all.
Subject matter doesn't exempt speech. Context is what shows this was a joke.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — True threats · jest and hyperbole

q: Vera's brother is burglarizing a neighbor's house. Watching from across the street, Vera texts him: “Neighbor's car just left, coast is clear.” She is charged as an accomplice to the burglary and argues that her text was truthful speech protected by the First Amendment. What result?
o: She has no First Amendment defense: speech that helps someone commit a crime is integral to it and unprotected.
Her text is protected unless it meets Brandenburg's test for incitement to imminent lawless action.
Her text is protected because it conveyed only true, factual information.
Her text is protected because private text messages are beyond the government's reach.
oe: Correct. Speech integral to crime includes speech that helps commit or conceal a crime, like “I'll tell you when the coast is clear.” It is unprotected whether written or spoken (Giboney and its progeny).
Brandenburg governs advocacy. Aiding and abetting is a separate unprotected category.
Truth doesn't protect speech that is part of a crime.
The medium doesn't matter. Speech integral to crime is unprotected, written or spoken.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — Speech integral to crime

q: A federal statute punishes anyone who “promotes” child pornography. Three people post online. Abe writes: “Child-pornography laws are an overreach; possession should be legal.” Bea writes: “I encourage everyone to go find this material for themselves.” Cal writes: “I have a folder of real videos of 10-year-olds. Message me and I'll send it.” Under Williams, whose speech can the statute constitutionally reach?
o: Only Cal's, because only he offers to transfer particular material.
Bea's and Cal's, because urging others to obtain contraband is solicitation of a crime.
All three, because speech about child pornography has de minimis value under Ferber.
None, because offers to provide material are protected unless the material is proved to exist.
oe: Correct. Williams construed “promotes” to mean recommending a particular piece of material with intent to initiate its transfer. It doesn't reach “child pornography should be legal” or even “I encourage you to obtain it,” which are abstract advocacy (Brandenburg; Claiborne Hardware).
Williams said “I encourage you to obtain it” is outside the statute; it names no particular material.
Ferber concerned the material itself, not speech about it. Advocating a change in the law is protected.
Offers to provide contraband are categorically unprotected, and the material needn't exist (Williams).
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — Offers vs. advocacy

q: Variation: Cal's message instead says, “These are AI-generated. No real kids were involved,” and he believes that is true. The statute, like the one upheld in Williams, covers material offered “in a manner that reflects the belief, or that is intended to cause another to believe,” that it depicts real minors. Can Cal be convicted under it?
o: No, because he neither believed nor claimed that real children were depicted.
Yes, because any offer of sexually explicit images of minors, real or virtual, is speech integral to crime.
Yes, because the government can't prove which images involve real children, so it may ban all of them.
No, because offers and requests are protected speech whatever the material is.
oe: Correct. Williams upheld punishing offers based on the belief or representation that real children are depicted, even if the belief is mistaken. Without that belief or representation, the offer concerns virtual images, which Free Speech Coalition protects.
An offer is integral to crime only if the material itself is unprotected, and virtual images aren't, unless obscene.
That difficulty is why Williams allowed punishing a mistaken belief, not a reason virtual images lost protection.
Offers of contraband are unprotected. The problem here is that the material isn't contraband.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — Pandering · belief
pre: A federal statute punishes anyone who “promotes” child pornography. Three people post online. Abe writes: “Child-pornography laws are an overreach; possession should be legal.” Bea writes: “I encourage everyone to go find this material for themselves.” Cal writes: “I have a folder of real videos of 10-year-olds. Message me and I'll send it.” Under Williams, whose speech can the statute constitutionally reach?

q: A small press publishes a step-by-step manual for poisoning someone without detection, marketed with the slogan “for readers ready to act.” Families of victims killed by a buyer who followed it exactly sue the publisher for aiding and abetting. In discovery they obtain the publisher's internal email: “Our buyer is someone planning a hit, so make the instructions foolproof.” The publisher moves to dismiss on First Amendment grounds. What result?
o: The claim can proceed, given evidence of intent to assist and use exactly as intended.
Dismissal, because a book is protected expression no matter how its readers use it.
Dismissal, because liability for speech requires imminent lawless action under Brandenburg.
Dismissal, because Paladin's rule applies only where the publisher stipulates to its intent.
oe: Correct. Rice v. Paladin allowed aiding-and-abetting liability where the publisher intended to assist murderers and the book was used exactly as intended. Intent was stipulated there; here, the email supplies evidence of intent beyond the text.
Paladin held that publishing is not exempt from aiding-and-abetting liability.
Aiding and abetting is speech integral to crime, a different category from incitement.
The stipulation was how intent was proved in Paladin, not an element of the rule.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — Aiding and abetting by publication

q: Variation: There is no email or any other evidence of the publisher's intent beyond the book itself, which is sold in general bookstores and bought mostly by mystery writers, toxicologists, and true-crime readers. What is the most likely result?
o: Liability is doubtful: without evidence beyond the text, the book looks like general information with legitimate readers.
Liability follows, because a book of detailed criminal instructions is unprotected whatever the publisher intended.
Liability follows, because Stevens lets courts recognize new categories for especially dangerous information.
Liability is barred, because published books, like news reporting, can't be a basis for liability.
oe: Correct. Paladin said intent evidence will almost never exist apart from stipulations, and copycat cases differ. The bomb-manual problem suggests requiring specific intent shown by evidence beyond the text; general publication to legitimate readers isn't a one-to-one offer.
Paladin rested on intent; detailed instructions alone weren't enough.
Stevens forbids creating new categories by balancing.
Paladin said news reporting is never a basis, but it allowed liability for a manual published with intent to assist.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — General-audience instructions
pre: A small press publishes a step-by-step manual for poisoning someone without detection, marketed with the slogan “for readers ready to act.” Families of victims killed by a buyer who followed it exactly sue the publisher for aiding and abetting. In discovery they obtain the publisher's internal email: “Our buyer is someone planning a hit, so make the instructions foolproof.” The publisher moves to dismiss on First Amendment grounds. What result?

q: An AI companion app is sued for wrongful death after a teenage user dies by suicide following months of intense use. The complaint alleges a manipulative, human-like design marketed to minors. The company moves to dismiss, arguing that its chatbot's output is the company's own protected speech. Under the reasoning of Garcia v. Character Technologies, what is the most likely ruling?
o: The motion may fail: the output may not reflect any person's expressive choice.
Dismissal, because any output made of words is speech protected by the First Amendment.
Dismissal, because the First Amendment bars tort suits based on the content of words.
Denial, because companies have no First Amendment protection for software.
oe: Correct. Garcia, relying on Justice Barrett's Moody v. NetChoice concurrence, wasn't prepared to hold that chatbot output is speech: an algorithm carrying out a human's expressive choice may be speech, but a language model generating its own output may not be.
Garcia held that output counts as speech only if it is expressive.
Speech integral to crime and other categories can support liability (Paladin), and Garcia doubted this was speech at all.
Garcia didn't say that; an algorithm carrying out a human's expressive choice may be speech.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — Is AI output speech?

q: Variation: Instead of claiming the output as its own speech, the company argues that its users have a First Amendment right to receive the chatbot's output, and it asserts that right on their behalf. How did Garcia treat this argument?
o: The company may assert its users' right to receive speech, but the output still counts only if it is expressive.
The company may not assert users' rights, because only listeners themselves can assert a right to receive speech.
Asserting users' rights wins the case, because a listener's right to receive information is absolute.
Asserting users' rights forfeits the defense, because it concedes the company made no expressive choice.
oe: Correct. Garcia let the distributor assert its users' rights as listeners, but that didn't answer whether chatbot output is speech at all.
Garcia allowed a distributor to assert its users' right to receive speech.
Listener rights are recognized but not absolute, and they depend on there being speech to receive.
The court didn't treat the argument as a forfeiture; it simply left the speech question unresolved.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — Listener rights
pre: An AI companion app is sued for wrongful death after a teenage user dies by suicide following months of intense use. The complaint alleges a manipulative, human-like design marketed to minors. The company moves to dismiss, arguing that its chatbot's output is the company's own protected speech. Under the reasoning of Garcia v. Character Technologies, what is the most likely ruling?

q: An 18-year-old posts a drill-rap verse on a public video site that names a rival rapper and describes shooting him outside a particular recording studio. The rival sees the video, fears for his safety, and stops going to that studio. The rapper is charged with making threats and argues that violent imagery is a convention of the genre. Under Counterman, which approach should the court take?
o: Weigh genre and context in deciding whether a reasonable recipient would see a threat, and require recklessness.
Dismiss, because song lyrics are artistic expression, which is protected from threat prosecutions.
Convict if the rival reasonably felt afraid, without regard to what the rapper knew or intended.
Convict only if the rapper intended the rival to fear violence, as incitement requires intent.
oe: Correct. The objective element is context-sensitive (genre, audience, medium, history between the parties), and Counterman adds a subjective floor of recklessness. Justice Sotomayor worried specifically about prosecutions over violent lyrics.
There's no categorical exemption; context determines whether a work conveys a true threat.
A purely objective standard was the Counterman dissent's view; the majority requires recklessness.
That was Justice Sotomayor's concurrence; the majority held that recklessness suffices.
topic: Ch. 5 · Threats & speech integral to crime — True threats · art and context

q: A state bans sending unsolicited text messages that advertise condoms or at-home HIV tests to any phone number in the state. It cites two interests: shielding recipients from offensive messages, and helping parents control what their children see on family phones. The ads aren't obscene. An advertiser sues. What is the most likely result?
o: The ban is invalid: offense to adults counts for little, and parents' interest can't justify it.
The ban is valid, because phones, like broadcasting, are uniquely pervasive and accessible to children.
The ban is valid, because advertising for sexual products gets no First Amendment protection.
The ban is valid, because phone users can't avoid unsolicited texts and so are a captive audience.
oe: Correct. Bolger: outside obscenity, offensiveness doesn't justify suppression, and the short trip from mailbox to trash can (here, the delete button) is an acceptable burden. Helping parents is a substantial interest, but government “may not reduce the adult population” to what is fit for children.
Pacifica's rationale is narrow and tied to broadcasting. Bolger refused to extend it to the mail.
Bolger protected contraceptive advertising.
Mail recipients weren't a captive audience in Bolger, and deleting a text is a minimal burden.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech: protecting adults — Protecting adults from offense

q: A state makes it a misdemeanor to display a bumper sticker containing “any profane word.” Nell is cited for a sticker reading “[Expletive] Gas Prices.” The state argues that drivers stuck in traffic behind her are a captive audience who can't avoid the sticker, and that many cars carry children. What result?
o: The law is invalid: profanity is protected, and other drivers can simply look away.
The law is valid, because drivers stuck behind her can't avoid the sticker and so are a captive audience.
The law is valid, because a profane word on display is a form of fighting words aimed at other drivers.
The law is valid under Pacifica, because children are likely to see the sticker.
oe: Correct. Cohen: unwilling viewers can “avoid further bombardment of their sensibilities simply by averting their eyes.” Calling speech profane doesn't make it restrictable.
A glance at a bumper sticker is like seeing Cohen's jacket in a courthouse corridor; viewers can look away.
Profanity that isn't a direct personal insult isn't fighting words (Cohen).
Pacifica is a narrow broadcasting exception, not a general power to purge public places of profanity.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech: protecting adults — Profanity

q: At 3 p.m. on a weekday, a broadcast television station airs a comedian's routine full of vulgar descriptions of sexual acts. The routine isn't obscene. After complaints from parents whose children were watching, the FCC issues an order finding the broadcast indecent. The station challenges the order. What is the most likely result?
o: The order is likely upheld: broadcasting is uniquely pervasive and accessible to children, and the time of day matters.
The order is invalid, because profanity and vulgarity are protected speech under Cohen.
The order is invalid, because only obscene speech may be regulated, and this routine isn't obscene.
The order is likely upheld, because government may restrict indecent speech in any medium children can reach.
oe: Correct. Pacifica upheld an FCC order about an afternoon broadcast of indecent but not obscene material. It rests on a nuisance rationale in which context (time of day, content, medium) is all-important: a “pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.”
Pacifica is the narrow exception to that principle for broadcasting.
Pacifica allowed regulation of broadcasts that are indecent but not obscene.
Pacifica is limited to broadcasting. Bolger refused to extend it to the mail.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech: protecting adults — Indecent broadcasts

q: Variation: The same routine is posted on a subscription streaming service that requires an account and a password, and a state law makes it a crime to stream indecent material. What is the most likely result?
o: Likely invalid, because Pacifica's rationale is tied to broadcasting.
Likely valid, because Pacifica allows regulation of indecent material in any electronic medium.
Likely valid, because children sometimes use their parents' accounts.
Likely valid, because a criminal ban is a gentler tool than the FCC order upheld in Pacifica.
oe: Correct. Pacifica stressed that broadcasting is uniquely pervasive and accessible to children and that unconsenting adults may tune in without warning. A subscription service requires a choice, and the law is a content-based restriction on adults' speech.
Pacifica's holding is narrow and specific to broadcasting.
Parents control access to the account, and Bolger rejects reducing adults to what is fit for children.
A criminal ban is harsher, and Pacifica expressly didn't decide whether criminal prosecution would be allowed.

After complaints from parents whose children were watching, the FCC issues an order finding the broadcast indecent. The station challenges the order. What is the most likely result?

q: During a live morning radio interview, a guest blurts out a single expletive before the host cuts him off. The state prosecutes the station's owner under a criminal statute banning “indecent broadcasts,” relying on Pacifica. Which is the best assessment?
o: Pacifica doesn't settle it; the Court left fleeting expletives and criminal cases open.
Pacifica squarely controls, because any indecent word on the radio is uniquely accessible to children.
The prosecution is valid, because a single expletive is obscene when broadcast.
The prosecution is invalid, because Cohen forbids any regulation of broadcast language.
oe: Correct. Pacifica upheld a declaratory order about a deliberate, repetitive monologue aired at 2 p.m. It expressly left open two-way radio, an occasional expletive, and criminal prosecution, all of which cut toward protection here.
Pacifica stressed context and the repetitive monologue, and it reserved the occasional expletive.
Obscenity requires all three Miller prongs; an expletive isn't a depiction of sexual conduct that appeals to prurient interest.
Pacifica allows some regulation of broadcast indecency; it just doesn't reach this far.

q: In an obscenity prosecution of a magazine publisher, the judge instructs the jury that material appeals to the “prurient interest” if it “tends to arouse ordinary, healthy sexual desire in the average person.” The jury convicts. What is the strongest argument on appeal?
o: The instruction misstates Miller: prurient interest means a shameful or morbid interest in sex, not a normal one.
Obscenity is protected speech, so the prosecution should have been dismissed.
The jury should have applied national standards, not community standards, to the prurient-interest prong.
The instruction was proper, but the jury should have judged each page of the magazine separately.
oe: Correct. Brockett v. Spokane Arcades: prurient interest means “a shameful or morbid interest in nudity, sex, or excretion,” not a normal interest in sex. An instruction that sweeps in ordinary sexual desire reaches protected speech.
Obscenity is unprotected under Miller, which is still good law.
Miller's first prong uses contemporary community standards.
Miller judges the work taken as a whole, not page by page.

q: A state amends its obscenity law to cover “material depicting graphic violence that, taken as a whole, appeals to a morbid interest in gore and lacks serious value.” A bookseller is prosecuted for selling a horror novel to an adult. What result?
o: The amendment is invalid, because obscenity is limited to depictions of sex.
The amendment is valid, because it borrows Miller's “taken as a whole” and “serious value” safeguards.
The amendment is valid for sales to adults but not for sales to minors.
The amendment is valid, because a morbid interest in gore is the same thing as a prurient interest.
oe: Correct. Brown: obscenity is confined to depictions of sexual conduct, and violent imagery is protected. Following Stevens, legislatures can't add categories by balancing value against harm.
Borrowing Miller's wording doesn't stretch the category beyond sexual conduct.
This gets it backward. Brown protected violent material even for minors, and adults are entitled to it too.
Prurient interest concerns sex (Brockett), not violence.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech: protecting adults — Obscenity covers sex, not violence

q: A county bans “sexually explicit films that depict people with disabilities as objects of ridicule or degradation,” whatever the films' artistic, political, or literary value. Sued by a filmmaker, the county defends the ban as a regulation of obscenity. Is that defense persuasive?
o: No. It skips Miller's elements and targets a viewpoint.
Yes, because sexually explicit material is obscene whenever it degrades a vulnerable group.
Yes, because the county's interest in protecting disabled people from subordination is compelling.
No, but only because the county failed to make legislative findings about the films' harms.
oe: Correct. Like the Indianapolis ordinance in Hudnut, the ban has no prurient-interest, offensiveness, community-standards, or work-as-a-whole inquiry, and value is irrelevant to it. It bans one perspective, which is viewpoint discrimination.
Degradation isn't a Miller element; the test is prurient interest, patent offensiveness, and lack of serious value.
Hudnut accepted that such depictions cause real harm and still struck the ordinance.
Findings wouldn't help; the problem is how the ban is built.

q: A city zoning ordinance requires adult movie theaters to be at least 1,000 feet from schools, churches, and homes. The city relies on studies from other cities showing that such theaters attract crime and lower property values. A theater operator argues that the ordinance is content-based and must satisfy strict scrutiny. What standard most likely applies?
o: Intermediate scrutiny, because the ordinance targets secondary effects like crime and property values, not the films' message.
Strict scrutiny, because the ordinance applies only to theaters showing sexually explicit films.
Rational basis, because adult films are unprotected obscenity.
Strict scrutiny, because the city relied on studies from other cities rather than its own.
oe: Correct. Renton: zoning laws that confine adult businesses get intermediate scrutiny, even though partly content-based, because they target secondary effects. The doctrine is narrow and hasn't been extended beyond adult entertainment.
Renton treated such zoning as aimed at secondary effects despite its content-based trigger.
Non-obscene adult films are protected, which is why some scrutiny applies.
Where the studies came from doesn't change the standard of review.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech: protecting adults — Secondary effects

q: Variation: The city instead bans adult theaters everywhere within its limits. The ordinance's preamble says the films “corrupt the morals of adult viewers,” and the city offers no evidence about crime or property values. What result?
o: Likely invalid: shielding adults from non-obscene content isn't a permissible goal.
Likely valid under Renton, because adult theaters may be regulated more strictly than other businesses.
Likely valid, because protecting public morality is a compelling interest.
Likely invalid, but only because a total ban leaves no alternative locations.
oe: Correct. Ask who is being protected and from what harm: here, adults, from the content itself. Government almost never may restrict immoral speech for that reason; obscenity, narrowly defined, is the exception. With no secondary effects, Renton doesn't apply.
Renton depends on a secondary-effects rationale, which this ordinance disclaims.
Bolger and Cohen hold that shielding adults from offensive content counts for little.
The deeper flaw is the moral purpose, which alone takes the case outside Renton.

q: A state makes it a crime to distribute photographs depicting sexual conduct by anyone under 17, whether or not the photographs are obscene. A gallery owner who sells a coming-of-age art book containing such photographs of real 15-year-olds argues that the book has serious artistic value, so it isn't obscene under Miller and can't be banned. What result?
o: The conviction stands, because Ferber doesn't require obscenity.
The conviction is reversed, because the state must satisfy all three Miller prongs, including lack of serious value.
The conviction is reversed, because the state may punish those who make the photographs but not those who sell them.
The conviction stands, but only because the book appeals to a prurient interest.
oe: Correct. Ferber: child pornography made with real children is unprotected regardless of Miller. Circulating it worsens the harm of a permanent record, and closing the distribution network may be the only practical way to dry up production. Its value is “exceedingly modest, if not de minimis.”
Ferber held that child pornography needn't be obscene to be unprotected.
Ferber stressed that the distribution network must be closed to control production.
Prurient appeal is a Miller element; Ferber doesn't require it.

q: A federal statute bans sexually explicit images of anyone who “appears to be” under 18. A studio releases a serious film about teenage life in which actors aged 22 and 24, made up to look 16, perform a brief explicit scene. The studio is prosecuted. What result?
o: Unconstitutional, because no real child was involved in making the film.
Constitutional, because images of apparent minors feed the same market as real child pornography.
Constitutional, because the government can't tell real minors from adult look-alikes, so it may ban both.
Constitutional, because a single explicit scene makes the whole film unprotected.
oe: Correct. Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition: Ferber doesn't extend to images made without real children, including adults who look like minors. The law bans speech regardless of its value.
The Court rejected this indirect-harm theory; Ferber's rationale depended on harm to real children in production.
That evidentiary concern later supported Williams's belief-based pandering rule, not a ban on look-alike images.
The artistic merit of a work “does not depend on the presence of a single explicit scene.”

q: Variation: One of the actors in the explicit scene is in fact 16 years old. What result?
o: The film may be punished as child pornography: a real child was used, and the work's value doesn't matter under Ferber.
It remains protected, because the film taken as a whole has serious artistic value.
It remains protected, because Free Speech Coalition protects sexually explicit films about teenagers.
It may be punished only if it also meets Miller's test for obscenity.
oe: Correct. Once a real minor takes part in the sexual conduct depicted, Ferber's rationale applies directly, whatever the film's artistic value.
Value saves a work under Miller, not under Ferber.
Free Speech Coalition protected images made without real children.
Ferber held that child pornography needn't be obscene.

q: A state requires commercial websites on which more than a third of the content is sexual material obscene as to minors to verify every visitor's age using government ID or transaction data. Adult users sue, arguing that filters on home devices would protect children with less burden on adults, as the Court found in Ashcroft v. ACLU. What standard most likely applies, and what result?
o: Intermediate scrutiny, which the law likely survives despite the filtering alternative.
Strict scrutiny under Ashcroft II, and the law fails because filters are less restrictive and at least as effective.
Rational basis, because material that is obscene as to minors is unprotected.
The law is invalid, because verification exposes adult users to privacy risks and stigma.
oe: Correct. Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton: age verification to keep minors from material obscene as to them burdens adults only incidentally, so intermediate scrutiny applies. Less restrictive alternatives like filters don't defeat a legitimate legislative choice under that standard.
Paxton distinguished the earlier cases as involving effective bans on adult access; the filtering argument lost under the lower standard.
Paxton rejected rational basis because adults have a real, if incidentally burdened, right to the material.
Paxton found privacy protected by the incentives of sites and verifiers, and stigma has never exempted the industry from regulation.
