q: Variation: The law instead makes it a crime to post any material harmful to minors on a commercial website. Its only safe harbor is an affirmative defense for sites that verify age by credit card, and the record shows that many adults lack credit cards and minors easily evade the check. Which framework most likely applies?
o: Strict scrutiny, as in Ashcroft II, because the law works as a ban on adults.
Intermediate scrutiny, as in Paxton, because any law with an age-verification feature burdens adults only incidentally.
Rational basis, because the material is harmful to minors.
No scrutiny, because Paxton overruled Ashcroft II and approved every online age-verification scheme.
oe: Correct. Paxton framed Reno and Ashcroft II as involving laws that effectively banned speech to adults. A criminal ban with an illusory verification defense looks like those laws, and Ashcroft II put the burden on the government to show that filters wouldn't work as well.
Paxton turned on the burden being incidental. A criminal ban with an illusory defense burdens adults directly.
Adults have a right to receive such material, so rational basis is out (Paxton).
Paxton distinguished Ashcroft II rather than overruling it; whether it effectively did so is an open question.

q: A state bans selling to anyone under 17 “horror novels depicting dismemberment or torture.” It relies on studies showing that teens who read such books are slightly more aggressive. The ban doesn't cover violent movies, cartoons, or video games. A bookseller sues. What result?
o: The ban is invalid: violent material is protected for minors, and the law fails strict scrutiny.
The ban is valid, because Ginsberg lets states adjust the obscenity category for minors.
The ban is valid, because minors have no First Amendment right to receive violent material.
The ban is valid, because books, unlike video games, aren't interactive and so get less protection.
oe: Correct. Brown: there's no new unprotected category for violence, even for minors, who have their own First Amendment rights. California's studies showed correlation and tiny effects, and its law was wildly underinclusive, which alone defeated it.
Ginsberg adjusted an existing category, obscenity, which covers sexual conduct only. California sought a new category for violence, and Brown rejected it.
Minors have a significant measure of First Amendment protection; there's no “free-floating power to restrict the ideas to which children may be exposed.”
Books are classic protected speech, and Brown treated interactivity as a difference of degree, not of kind.

q: Variation: The state instead bans in-store sales to anyone under 17 of sexually explicit magazines that are obscene as to minors, applying the Miller test adjusted for minors. Adults may still buy them. What result?
o: The ban is likely valid: keeping material obscene as to minors from them is a traditional power that adjusts an existing category.
The ban is invalid under Brown, because minors have a First Amendment right to receive sexual material.
The ban is invalid under Bolger, because it reduces adults to reading only what is fit for children.
The ban is valid, because sexually explicit magazines are unprotected for adults as well.
oe: Correct. Ginsberg v. New York let states adjust obscenity for minors, and Paxton reaffirmed that power. Brown distinguished Ginsberg because it adjusted an existing category rather than creating a new one.
Brown protected violent material. States may keep material that is obscene as to minors away from minors.
Adults may still buy the magazines; only sales to minors are barred.
Non-obscene sexually explicit material is protected for adults.

q: A 24-year-old man persuades a 15-year-old girl he met online to send him explicit photos of herself, which he saves. Charged with soliciting and possessing child pornography, he argues that she made the images herself, so no one exploited her in producing them, and that Ferber's market rationale doesn't fit. What is the best response?
o: Ferber's rationale fits: an adult solicited images of a real child.
He's right: self-produced images fall outside Ferber, so the state must prove the photos are obscene.
He's right, because the girl agreed to send the images, and her consent makes them protected.
The charges can stand only if he passed the images on to others, creating the circulation Ferber worried about.
oe: Correct. The teen-sexting problem suggests a rule that turns on exploitation: consensual exchange between peers fits Ferber poorly, but an adult partner looks like Ferber. And requests to obtain such material are unprotected (Williams).
The self-produced framing fits poorly when an adult solicited the images; that's the exploitation Ferber targets.
A 15-year-old's consent doesn't take the images outside Ferber where an adult induced them.
Requests to obtain such material are themselves unprotected (Williams), and Ferber's rationale doesn't depend on redistribution.
